Q: My cat is 11. Is she a senior, and how often should she see the vet?
A: Yes. Feline guidelines call cats seniors once they are over 10 years old.

Older cats are good at hiding illness, so regular checks matter. Many vets suggest a visit every 6 months, with blood tests, a urine test and a blood pressure check at least once a year. Cats with health problems may need visits more often.

Common problems in older cats include kidney disease, an overactive thyroid, high blood pressure, diabetes, arthritis and dental disease.

Tell your vet if you notice weight loss, drinking or peeing more, changes in eating, litter box accidents, hiding, or crying at night.

Q: My dog is peeing everywhere He's nine years old, but he suddenly started peeing on the leg of a chair in a certain room, the backroom on a gift bag, and the corner of my rug by my bed. I …
A: There is a reason why your dog has started to urinate everywhere, and whether that reason is behavioural or medical, you need to take him to a veterinarian.

There are many possible medical causes, ranging from a urinary tract infection, joint pain, metabolic disease (diabetes or Cushing's), prostatic disease (since he is intact), to something more sinister. Equally well the inappropriate urination may be a behavioural issue, such as marking behaviour or anxiety due to a change to his environment.

Either way your veterinarian will need to rule out a medical cause, and at minimum will likely want to do bloodwork (CBC and chemistry) as well as a urinalysis, and may want to do pursue imaging.

Q: When do we need cat nets on window?

Sometimes I see windows with a cat net installed on it. How are they used? When should I consider using a cat net?
A: Any fall over 10 feet/4 meters could be dangerous to a cat. (Websearch "feline high-rise syndrome" for statistics). Cats may be OK above that, or may be at risk below that, but that's the point at which I would start worrying. (A past cat almost stuck her landing from 15', but banged her jaw on the ground and broke it.)

As with kids, the risk depends in part on how careful the cat is or isn't, but sudden wind gusts or a misstep are always a risk.

Insect screens aren't adequate to protect kids, but can do a decent job of protecting most cats, and are probably more useful and more attractive than netting...?

Q: What happens if cats drink coffee? I was drinking my coffee the other day and I accidentally spilled some on the floor (a couple of drops). My cat licked them. I don't really think this is a big deal because …
A: Caffeine is very bad for cats and dogs. Don't let your cats have any coffee, soda, tea, etc.

One tiny dose won't kill them, but you could be racking up organ damage each time. The HCCUA health website states that cats will get heart and nervous system damage from caffeine. I imagine it would also hurt the liver, kidneys, and GI tract as well.

Plants make caffeine to kill off any creatures eating the plants. Alkaloids (caffeine is an alkaloid) are intended to kill off anything that eats them, not just insects. Humans and other plant-eating animals have developed defenses to common alkaloids, which is why people aren't really affected by caffeine. Cats and dogs have no such defenses.

Q: My dog is limping. What should I do?
A: Limping usually means pain or weakness, so it deserves a vet check.

First aid at home:
- Keep him calm and limit his activity.
- Gently check the paw for cuts, a broken nail, or something stuck between the toes. Stop if he shows pain. Dogs in pain may bite, even their owners.
- Don't give human pain medicines unless your vet tells you to. They can poison pets.

Go to the vet now if he:
- Won't put any weight on the leg, or the leg looks bent or swollen
- Can't stand or walk without help
- Was hit by a vehicle or attacked by another animal
- Is in severe pain, or the limp came on suddenly and badly

See your vet within 24 hours if the limp lasts more than a day or is getting worse. A short video of him walking at home helps the vet.

Q: pwede ba i-walk ang aso ko without a leash?
A: Not in public. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must keep their dogs under control and not let them roam public places without a leash. LGUs must also make sure dogs are leashed or kept inside the owner's property (Section 7).

The implementing rules add:
- The leash should be no longer than 1.5 meters
- The dog tag should be on the collar or harness
- Aggressive dogs should wear a muzzle in public

The law sets a fine of P500 per incident for not leashing a dog outside the house (Section 11). These amounts are as written in the 2007 law. Your city or municipality may have its own ordinance, so check with your city or municipal veterinary office.

Q: What are the signs of rabies in a dog or cat?
A: The DOH lists these signs of rabies in animals:

- Change in behavior
- Aggressive behavior
- Excessive drooling
- Paralysis
- Fear of water

You can't confirm rabies just by looking at an animal; only a lab test can. If your pet shows these signs, keep away from its saliva, keep it confined, and call your vet or city or municipal veterinary office right away. If it bit or scratched anyone, they should go to an Animal Bite Treatment Center.

Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

Instead:
- Move your pet away from the poison.
- Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now and go in.
- Bring the package, label or a photo, and note what was eaten, how much and when.
- If it's on the skin or fur, wash with mild soap and water.

On the way, keep your pet calm and watch the breathing. Some poisons cause delayed signs, so go even if your pet seems fine.

Q: Why do dogs lick faces?

Why do dogs lick people and other dogs in their faces?
A: Domesticated dogs inherited this trait primarily from wolves, and more specifically, wolf pups. Wolf pups will lick the faces of their mother to try and induce her to vomit some of her last meal. For a weaning pup this is far easier for them to digest and eat than meat and bones right from a carcass.

Source

Part of the selective breeding that went into creating the domesticated dog species thousands of years ago involved breeding of more timid wolves and wolves that exhibited more puppy like behavior. Most adult wolves would have an untenable and difficult relationship with humans so a more fitting companion to a human would be a wolf that is less aggressive and more willing to follow the human pack.

Other wolf puppy behaviors that dogs carried is play. Adult wolves rarely play while wolf pups play consistently as a means of learning.

Q: Should my cat follow daylight savings? I feed my cat twice a day: once in the morning and once in the evening. He is of the type that is always willing to eat, so I try and maintain a strict …
A: According to various pet behaviourists, dogs' Circadian rhythms are generally set around the amount of daylight rather than time, as they lack the ability to differentiate between say, 6 PM and 7 PM the way humans do. This is mitigated some by the artificial light cycles (you turning lights on and off, etc) in your home.

Your pet might notice the change and will likely take a bit to adjust, but generally they do adjust to the differences (in daylight, timing, etc.) which come with Daylight Savings time.

If you like, you can choose to slowly adjust the pet's schedule, but generally the pet should be okay with the time change. Like humans, pets will need time to adjust, but they generally figure it out.

Q: Can I get sick from my cats sharing my food or drink? My cat loves to drink out of my water glass. We don't try to encourage the behavior, but sometimes she sneaks a sip while we're not looking. She …
A: The short answer is yes.

The longer answer is that while, for the most part, there aren't many zoonotic diseases that can transfer from cats to humans, there are some infections that can be transmitted from the cat to you through shared sources, notably protozoal infections. These are basically single-celled organisms that can cause severe diarrhea in both humans and cats and are normally contracted from the same sources (e.g. tainted water). However, depending on the cat and its habits they may be drinking water you are not, such as toilet water, and so it's possible that it taints your water via transfer.

Also, the great indoors is not always isolated from the great outdoors. Mice and other small rodents, along with insects, can also enter the premises and they may contaminate things that, in turn, get picked up by the cat. The Center for Disease Control has a list of possible infections that could arise.

Q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
A: Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Wash entire box once a week: remove litter, wash box and refill.

Q: My dog suddenly collapsed and isn't responding to me.
A: This needs a vet immediately. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic and leave right away.

Quick checks:
- Breathing: watch whether the chest rises and falls.
- Heartbeat: put your hand flat on the chest to feel for it.

If there's no breathing or heartbeat, ask the clinic on the phone to guide you through chest compressions. Keep going until your dog breathes on his own or the vet takes over.

On the way:
- Have someone else drive, especially if you're doing compressions.
- Lay him on a firm, flat surface and keep his head level and neck straight.
- Be careful when he wakes up, since a confused dog may bite.

Q: What does 5-in-1 or 6-in-1 vaccine mean?
A: The number tells you how many diseases one shot protects against. Combining them means fewer injections.

Labels often use letters, for example:
- D = distemper
- A2 = adenovirus type 2 (protects against hepatitis)
- P = parvovirus
- P = parainfluenza
- L = leptospirosis

So "DA2PP" covers four diseases, and adding L gives "DA2LPP". Products differ in what they add, such as extra lepto strains or other germs, so the number alone doesn't tell you the exact mix.

For cats, the common combo is FVRCP: feline viral rhinotracheitis (herpesvirus), calicivirus and panleukopenia.

Ask your vet which diseases your pet's vaccine card covers.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: Do spayed cats still spray?

If I get my indoor female cats spayed, will they no longer spray? Or will they just spray for territorial reasons only?
A: Any cat can spray if sufficiently motivated to. It is a natural response.

Spaying does, however, remove a very strong trigger for a female cat. Biology demands that she broadcast to tomcats that she is ready for breeding, so come and get it. After spaying, that motivation goes away entirely.

But spaying may also be a signal for other cats to stay away, a claiming of ownership. If this is the driving force, then spraying could persist until whatever causes this distress is handled in some way.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: My dog was bitten by a stray that might have rabies. What happens now?
A: Take your dog to a vet right away and tell them about the bite. The implementing rules of RA 9482 say:

- A previously vaccinated dog that can be identified should be revaccinated immediately and confined for at least 90 days
- A dog bitten by a suspected rabid or unknown animal should be confined under a vet's supervision for 6 months
- An unvaccinated dog bitten by a confirmed rabid animal must be put to sleep right away

Wear gloves if you need to handle wounds, and avoid contact with your dog's saliva. Your city or municipal veterinary office can guide you.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

A: The only mammals you'd be able to keep healthy on a vegetarian diet would be rabbits, or rodents like gerbils, hamsters, mice, rats, guinea pigs, etc. They will all do fine on a diet of vegetables and grains.

If you have the means to, you could keep an exotic pet like a fruit bat. But I would stress that bats are high maintenance, might require a license depending on where you live, and aren't able to be housebroken. The first question you have to ask is are you willing to have a bat fly around your house all night?

Otherwise you'll want to look into animals like birds, fish, or even a select few reptiles.

Other mammals are either carnivore (all meat), omnivore (some meat), or insectivore (almost all insects).

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: Managing litter box for cat with polyuria (increased urination)? As cats get older, they commonly develop conditions such as chronic kidney disease or diabetes which leads to polyuria (production of large amounts of urine). Managing the litter box in these …
A: More and/or larger boxes.

The standard guideline is one box per cat plus a spare. Cats with polyuria are like having more cats, so add more boxes accordingly. Spread the boxes around the house so older or ill cats don't have to walk as far and will be less tempted to go somewhere inappropriate.

Larger boxes will accommodate more litter and thus more waste. Standard litter boxes are often too small anyway, especially covered ones, and can rarely hold more than one day's waste from one healthy cat. A larger box will also be easier for an older or ill cat to move around and dig in. A high-sided box also helps with cats that don't (or can't) squat properly. Storage totes are cheap and work well, though perhaps not aesthetically pleasing.

Q: How do I train a dog to drop the ball after fetching? A neighbourhood dog that's gotten friendly comes over to visit us occasionally. He really loves playing fetch, and gets really excited if he sees me playing with a …
A: First you train the dog to come when called (there are many resources on the web that can teach you how to do that). Train that to the point where the dog will come very reliably. Next I would go with the "2nd ball" approach mentioned above. If the dog doesn't bring the ball to you, then call him to come and immediately throw the second ball when s/he comes to you. The dog will likely drop the ball right away as soon as you throw the ball. Once that is established the dog will likely start dropping the first ball at your feet in anticipation of the second ball being thrown. If not, then delay throwing the second ball until the first is dropped.

A: The loose, hanging skin on a cat's belly is simply a natural part of a cat's anatomy, sometimes called the apron, or as in the following article, the primordial pouch. Getting spayed or neutered does not cause your cat to gain an apron, but it may make it more obvious due to related changes in weight.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: Lily pollen got on my cat's fur and she drank water from the flower vase. Is she in danger?
A: Yes, treat this as an emergency. For cats, every part of true lilies and daylilies is poisonous, including the pollen and the vase water. Even a small amount licked off the fur can cause deadly kidney failure. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Early treatment makes a big difference. Waiting 18 hours or more often leads to kidney damage that can't be reversed.

Before you go:
- Wipe the pollen off her fur with a damp cloth so she can't lick more.
- Bring the flower or a photo so the vet can identify it.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to.

She may look fine at first. Early signs include drooling, vomiting, low energy and not eating. Keep lilies out of homes with cats.

A: The domestication of cats was a multi-step process like that of the dog coming from wolves. It seems to have taken place in the Fertile Crescent region of ancient Egypt. The friendliest of the wild cats would make a living by hanging out near human dwellings and killing the rats and mice that they found there. Although domestication was evident about 10,000 years ago, genetic studies show that the "wild cats" that gave rise to domestic cats branched off from their even wilder brethren about 130,000 years ago. Q: How can a cat go to the bathroom if he can't lift his tail? We accidentally ran into our cat backing out of our driveway. We took him to the vet and they said he broke many parts of his …
A: I think you've misunderstood the situation slightly.

A cat's tail is an extension of its spinal column, and the base of the spinal cord runs into it. Some of the nerves run back from the tail into the cat's hindquarters, including (if i'm remembering correctly) to the colon and anus. A tail injury, like any other spinal injury, risks damaging the central nervous system and causing loss of sensation or loss of control.

So the issue isn't one of whether the cat can lift its tail. It's whether the damage has affected the cat's ability to control some fairly essential muscles.

The good point here is that you should have an answer relatively quickly, either way.

Think about the cat's comfort and quality of life, and work with your vet to determine the best course of action. A possibly useful question to ask: "If this was your cat, what would you do?"

A: Burns are often worse than they look, because fur hides the damage. Large or deep burns, burns on the face, and any chemical or electrical burn need a vet right away. To be safe, go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: How often do you feed your cats?

I finally bought one of these automatic cat feeders and I’m in the process of programming it.

How often during the day should I feed the cats? They’re both older cats.
A: It depends on the cats and the style of feeder.

Some feeders let you pick how much food to dispense at each feeding. In that case, I would do half of their daily food budget in the morning and half in the evening, to match when cats are most active (and thus most hungry).

Other feeders can only deliver a fixed amount of food. In that case, you must set it to deliver that amount enough times per day to equal their daily food budget. I would still put one serving in the morning and one in the evening, and spread any extras needed in between during the day.

For completeness: the ideal of two feedings per day is for adult cats. Kittens need smaller meals every 4-6 hours, or just free feed them since kittens rarely need portion control.

Q: My dog got bitten by a snake in the yard. What should I do?
A: Treat any snake bite as an emergency and go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, even if the bite looks small. Some venoms, like cobra venom, cause little swelling but can affect breathing. Treatment works best when started early.

On the way:
- Keep your dog calm and limit his movement. Carry him if you can.
- Don't cut the bite, try to suck out the venom, or tie a tourniquet.
- Don't put ice, cold packs, heat or sprays on it.
- Don't wait to see if signs appear.

If the snake is already dead, you can bring it without damaging the head, which helps the vet identify it. Never try to catch a live snake. Call the clinic ahead so they can prepare.

Q: How often should I deworm my kitten?
A: Kittens often get roundworms from their mother's milk, so deworming starts early.

Parasite experts (CAPC) advise:
- Start at 2 weeks old
- Repeat every 2 weeks until your kitten starts a monthly year-round parasite preventive
- If a monthly preventive isn't used: every 2 weeks until 2 months old, then monthly until 6 months, then every 3 months
- Have the kitten's poop checked by the vet several times in the first year

Ask your vet for a product that suits your kitten's weight and age, and use only products made for cats.

messages.content:
Cat who is normally docile freaks out when a neighborhood cat comes onto our porch, despite getting along well with our other cats. Why?

Context

Our family has four cats. Some details about Pepe, the most relevant one to this question:
- 5 years old
- Orange tabby
- Male
- Exclusively indoors
- Properly fixed
- Extremely friendly and affectionate

Last fall we discovered, fostered, and then adopted a trio of stray kittens. At the time Pepe was scared of these kittens, often hiding in our rooms at the expense of his own well-being. That problem has since been resolved and he now gets along with the triplets very well.

Recently another male cat, whom we'll call T'Challa, has been walking around our neighborhood, including on our front porch. He's friendly, but we otherwise know very little about him; we're not even certain that he's stray.

The Problem

When T'Challa prowls around our yard or our porch, Pepe starts to get very defensive, even trying to attack him through the window. What confuses me is that this is extremely unlike him.

Some more facts about Pepe's behavior:
- He gets riled up to the extent that he'll force the triplets out of his way.
- When he calms down, he's friendly and affectionate again.
- He never behaves this way with the triplets. He plays or cuddles with them all the time.
- He's not ill or in pain.
- Their first interaction was apparently cordial, but I wasn't there so I couldn't tell you much more.

My question: what happened?

T'Challa is a tomcat and therefore a competitor for territory and females. Pepe is just defending his territory. Tomcats are generally more territorial than females and protect their territory more aggressively.

It could also be that Pepe and T'Challa met before and had a fight. Pepe remembers the cat and the fight and prepares himself for another fight.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: How to take care of my dog's teeth? My 2 year old dog is starting to have yellow teeth, especially the ones in the back of his jaws. I was wondering, what is the right way to take care of …
A: Here are a few options for you:

1) Brush your dogs teeth daily (once a week is not enough), or if he hates brushing then apply the paste directly onto his teeth.

2) Feed a dental diet such as Hill's T/D or Royal Canin Dental diet, if they aren't chewing the food then the diet itself is useless.

3) Dentastix, Greenies, CET chews, moderately soft chew toys (if you wack it on your knee and it hurts then it's too hard for your pets teeth) are all other good options for healthy teeth. If he eats the treats too fast or swallows them whole then it wont work.

Stay away from bones, sticks and hard chew toys, they will damage your dogs teeth or get lodged in their esophagus (sticks/bones).

Prevention is key as once periodontal disease sets in you cannot reverse it.

I'm concerned about her reaction to moving to a strange new place, especially if I were to leave immediately after. What is the least bad option for her?

I would move a week early. Going to a new place is traumatic for most cats, they need time to adjust and scent mark. As you said, boarding then new apartment would be doubly traumatic.

If there is not enough time to get used to her to get used to the apartment, why would it be any better with boarding? In a boarding situation, there will be all sorts of other cats and stimuli to stress her out. In your new home, she can feel relatively safe hiding under her bed :)

Even if she has been boarded there before, it is unlikely that she will occupy the same domicile with her own scent.

Q: My dog walked through insecticide our neighbor sprayed and now he's drooling and shaking.
A: This could be insecticide poisoning, which can get serious fast. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Signs from many bug sprays, such as organophosphates and carbamates, include heavy drooling, tiny pupils, vomiting, diarrhea, peeing a lot, trembling, weakness, trouble breathing and seizures.

Before and on the way:
- If he's breathing well and it won't delay you, wear gloves and gently wash his paws and coat with mild dish soap and lots of water. Don't scrub with a brush.
- If he's struggling to breathe, skip the bath and go straight away.
- Bring the product label, or ask the neighbor what was used.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't rub oil on him.

Keep pets off sprayed areas until they are dry.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: What are the signs of tick fever in dogs?
A: "Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: My dog is limping. What should I do?
A: Limping usually means pain or weakness, so it deserves a vet check.

First aid at home:
- Keep him calm and limit his activity.
- Gently check the paw for cuts, a broken nail, or something stuck between the toes. Stop if he shows pain. Dogs in pain may bite, even their owners.
- Don't give human pain medicines unless your vet tells you to. They can poison pets.

Go to the vet now if he:
- Won't put any weight on the leg, or the leg looks bent or swollen
- Can't stand or walk without help
- Was hit by a vehicle or attacked by another animal
- Is in severe pain, or the limp came on suddenly and badly

See your vet within 24 hours if the limp lasts more than a day or is getting worse. A short video of him walking at home helps the vet.

Q: How should I respond when my cat wants to wrestle? Sometimes when I am petting my 3-year-old cat she will roll over on her back and stretch out. At this point, if I bring my hand near she will try …
A: Playtime is an important bonding experience between you and your cat so you should take the opportunity to play!

However, if you let her play with your hand, you will teach her that hands are acceptable playtoys, and it will become difficult to later teach her not to bite or claw at your hands.

I would also recommend staying away from any toys that are hand shaped, such as padded gloves (some people will play with their cats using oven mitts or specially designed cat toy gloves). These items will also teach the cat that your hand is a toy.

A better idea is to use a toy that will establish a clear distance between your hand and her. Interactive wand toys such as Da Bird are usually a good choice.

Q: Can a dog that has had all his shots for parvo, still contract it? I have a 1.5 year old Boston terrier who when he was a puppy got all his shots, including 3 for parvo. My roommate recently got …
A: Parvovirus most commonly affects unvaccinated puppies less than 6 months of age. However, no vaccine is 100% effective, and vaccinated adult dogs can much less commonly be infected.

Even though the risk may be low in a vaccinated dog, I would still take your dog to see a veterinarian. They can perform a Parvovirus SNAP test. If your dog is in the early infection stages, he may not be shedding the virus in large quantities in the faeces yet. In this case your veterinarian may recommend a blood test (complete blood count). Since parvovirus typically affects the bone marrow first, a low white blood cell count could be an early indicator of infection.

Parvovirus can live in the environment for many months, so make sure to disinfect and clean all surfaces with a dilute bleach solution – especially toys, bowls, etc.

Q: I adopted an adult cat with no vaccine records. What should I do?
A: If you don't know a cat's vaccine history, vets treat the cat as unvaccinated. That usually means starting a fresh set of core vaccines, much like a kitten's first series.

For kittens, the series begins at 6 to 8 weeks and is repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until about 16 weeks. Your vet will decide how many doses your adult cat needs.

When you visit, ask about:
- Core vaccines (FVRCP and rabies)
- Testing for feline leukemia (FeLV) and FIV, especially if the cat lived outdoors
- Deworming and flea control

Book a vet visit within the first week after adoption.

Q: My Shih Tzu got into a fight and one eye looks like it's bulging out of the socket.
A: This is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. The longer the eye stays exposed, the more it dries out and gets damaged, which lowers the chance of saving his sight. Flat-faced breeds like Shih Tzus and Pugs are more prone to this.

On the way:
- Don't try to push the eye back in.
- Keep it moist if you can, for example with a clean cloth dampened with saline. Ask the clinic how when you call.
- Stop him from pawing or rubbing at it.
- Keep him calm and still.

For other eye injuries, also see a vet right away. Flush chemicals out with lots of water first, and never pull out an object stuck in the eye.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: Is it safe to put lavender oil on my dog's skin? If so, how should I dilute it? Is it safe to put lavender oil on my dog's skin? If so, please tell me the best way to dilute it …
A: Lavender oil is safe for dogs, cats and humans and does indeed repel fleas and ticks. Since it's the smell that repels fleas, you don't have to spread the oil over the whole body.

A very easy way to apply the oil is to rub a few drops onto the collar or bandana of your dog. The advantage is that the fur won't get oily and collect dirt.

Otherwise, rub the undiluted oil directly into the fur, one drop at a time. For small dogs one drop in the neck should suffice. For bigger dogs, add one drop to the top of their hips or the back of their hind legs, where they cannot lick it off. If your dog has very long fur, use more drops.

Repeat the treatment every few days when the oil has evaporated and your dog no longer smells like lavender.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: My senior dog seems confused and paces at night. What's wrong?
A: This can be a sign of cognitive dysfunction, a condition like dementia in people. It affects about 14 to 22% of dogs over 8 years old. Signs include:
- Getting lost or stuck in corners at home
- Sleeping more in the day and restless at night
- Less interest in family members
- Toilet accidents in the house
- Pacing, anxiety or barking for no clear reason

Cats can get it too, and often meow more.

Pain, vision loss and other illnesses can cause similar changes, so see your vet for a full check. Treatment works best when started early. Gentle exercise, new toys and simple games can help keep your pet's mind active.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: My cat always sleeps upside down

Whenever my cat goes to sleep,after a minute or so, it turns upside down (belly up)and there is some twitching in the paws legs tail and whiskers. Is it normal or some disease?
A: Entirely normal.

Some people prefer to sleep on their stomachs, others on their sides or backs; some change position depending on how warm or cold they are or for other reasons.

The same is true of cats. Upside down may look silly to us, but it really doesn't mean anything but that the cat is comfortable that way, and that it trusts you not to try to take advantage of this less-defended pose.

A bit of twitching of paws and face usually just indicates that the cat is dreaming.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: Can a pet legally be put to sleep in the Philippines?
A: Only for reasons the Animal Welfare Act allows. Section 6 of RA 8485 permits killing a pet when, for example:

- A licensed vet certifies it has an incurable communicable disease
- A licensed vet certifies it is needed to end the animal's suffering
- It is needed to prevent immediate danger to human life or limb

It must be done humanely, using methods approved by the Committee on Animal Welfare. Electrocution of dogs is banned under RA 9482. Talk to your vet if you're facing this decision.

Q: When does my puppy start his shots, and why so many?
A: Puppies usually get their first core vaccine at 6 to 8 weeks old. Shots are then repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is at least 16 weeks old.

Why a series? Antibodies from the mother's milk protect a young puppy, but they also block vaccines from working. These antibodies fade at a different age in each puppy, so repeat shots make sure one of them "takes". The dose given at 16 weeks or later is the most important.

Global guidelines also advise another core dose at around 6 months old instead of waiting until 1 year, to catch puppies that did not respond earlier.

Your vet will set the exact schedule for your puppy.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: Which vaccines are core for dogs?
A: Core vaccines are the ones every dog should get, wherever it lives. For dogs these protect against:
- Distemper
- Parvovirus
- Adenovirus (infectious hepatitis)

Rabies vaccine is also core anywhere the disease is present or the law requires it.

Global guidelines now say leptospirosis vaccine should be given to all dogs in places where the disease occurs, so in those areas it is treated as core too.

Other vaccines, like kennel cough (Bordetella and parainfluenza), are "non-core". Your vet suggests them based on your dog's lifestyle, such as boarding or contact with many dogs. Ask your vet which vaccines suit your dog.

Q: My cat keeps shaking her head and scratching her ears. Ear mites?
A: It could be. Ear mites are tiny parasites that live in the ear canal and are especially common in cats. Signs include:
- Head shaking

Q: How can I train my cat not to scratch furniture? How could I train my cat not to scratch everything while I need to go to school and my mother to work? I want educational advices that i could learn …
A: Your best option is to work with your cat's instincts, rather than against them. Cats have an instinct to scratch so you need to provide suitable objects for them to scratch on that are more attractive than your furniture. Buy (or make) several scratching posts, bait them with catnip, and place them around the house. Cats like to scratch when they wake up, so put scratching posts near favourite sleeping spots. Another good place is right next to any place your cat has a tendency to scratch (like the arm of a sofa).

Reward your kitten (with treats or praise) for using the scratching posts, and she will build good associations with sratching there. She will learn to prefer scratching on the surfaces you provide instead of your furniture.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

Q: My dog ate a chocolate bar. What should I do?
A: Chocolate is poisonous to dogs, especially dark and baking chocolate. Call or go to a vet now, even if your dog seems fine, because signs can take hours to show.

- Bring the wrapper if you can
- Don't make your dog vomit unless the vet tells you to

Q: Can dogs get sleep apnea? My dog is currently sleeping with her head on my leg, and snoring quite blissfully. While I am certain that she doesn't have apnea (she only snores occasionally, and, as a 74 pound adult Labrador …
A: Sleep Apnea isn't a disorder that is isolated to just humans. Dogs can also be affected by this disorder.

Cases of Sleep Apnea in dogs will result in drop in blood oxygen levels and interrupted sleep. This in itself isn't life or death but if this persist, it can lead to much more serious health conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, and heart diseases.

Noticeable symptoms of Sleep Apnea include
- Choking/gasping during sleep
- Loud chronic snoring
- Interrupted breathing with long pauses between breathes
- Sleepiness during day
- Irritability

Canine Sleep Apnea is also most common in dogs with flatter faces. Such as English bulldogs, pugs and Boston terriers. Overweight dogs also have higher chances of having Sleep Apnea.

Q: At what age is my dog considered a senior?
A: There's no single age, because dogs age at different rates depending on breed and size. Vets often call a dog senior when it is in the last quarter of its expected lifespan. As a rough guide, many dogs reach this stage at around 7 to 8 years.

From that age:
- See the vet at least twice a year
- Ask about blood and urine tests every 6 to 12 months to catch problems early
- Have blood pressure and thyroid checked yearly

Watch for changes at home, like slowing down, drinking more, weight change or confusion, and tell your vet. Old age is not a disease. Many changes can be treated.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: Why is my dog very protective with his treats? Whenever I give my dog a chewy bone treat he always protects it and acts like I am going to take it off him. He runs off and chews it alone …
A: "Protect his treat with his life" is probably a bit exaggerated.

It's just "just in case he'll take it!" behavior. This might also originate from you taking something else or it could be really just inherent behavior. There's nothing to worry about.

However, what you can try is really trivial and simple:
- Get your dog in a place where it has a hard time escaping with the bone.
- Give it the bone.
- After a moment (depends on how fast it'll finish it), take it again.
- Look at it a bit, let your dog see it, then give it back.
- Repeat this over a few days and the dog should become less "protective", since it will notice that you'll give it back.

These steps should also work in other instances of "protective behavior", e.g. the dog snarling or barking, if you try to take anything.

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

A: Split his daily portions. Cats are designed to have smaller, frequent meals.

Q: How can I tell if my cat has arthritis?
A: Cats hide pain well, but arthritis is very common in older cats. Studies show more than 60% have it in at least one joint. Signs are often subtle:
- Not jumping up as high, or hesitating before jumping
- Avoiding stairs
- Trouble getting in and out of the litter box, or going outside it
- Grooming less, so the coat looks messy
- Sleeping more and being less active

Ways to help at home:
- Use a litter box with a low side
- Add steps or ramps to favorite spots
- Keep her at a healthy weight

Ask your vet for a check. Never give your cat human pain medicine unless your vet says so.

Q: My cat swallowed one of my paracetamol (Biogesic) tablets that fell on the floor.
A: This is an emergency. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) can kill cats, and cats are far more sensitive to it than dogs. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. Don't wait for signs.

Signs can start within a few hours:
- Brown or muddy-coloured gums
- Fast or deep breathing, weakness
- Swelling of the face or paws
- Vomiting, or yellow eyes and gums

Before you go:
- Bring the medicine pack and note when it happened and how many tablets may be missing.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't give milk, food or any other medicine.

On the way, keep her calm in a carrier with good airflow. Keep all medicines where pets can't reach them.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: Can a regular German Shepherd give birth to German Shepherd puppies with coat colors identical to hers, but give birth to one single white puppy Just curious to know (I also need this piece of info for writing my novel). …
A: Yes it is possible! Not common, but it CAN happen.

The white coloring happens because of a recessive gene that can be hidden for several generations before making an appearance. Both parents must carry the white gene to produce white German Shepherd puppies.

It is very possible that two "normal colored" German Shepherds (carrying the white gene) can produce white puppies in a litter of black and tans or sables, etc.

A white German Shepherd is not albino, and should also have both dark eyes with a black nose and lips. White is also considered a "masking" gene which covers up the dog's true color, although it does not affect skin pigment. This is why "white" German Shepherds often have a cream or blond tint to their solid white coat.

Q: Why is my cat growling at the laser dot? I have recently gotten a laser pointer to play with my two cats (mother and son). The son is overweight and I thought the laser pointer would help with giving him …
A: Cats love laser pointers because they can see something you can't - the dot never stops moving. Cats are attracted to movement, it stimulates them. So, within the dot the light is constantly moving and stimulating them.

For this reason you have to be careful. Some cats will chase laser dots to their detriment. They will exhaust themselves. In hunting, cats are sprinters, not marathoners and to chase something for a prolonged period is not really in their nature. When they do, they can exhaust and injure themselves.

So what is probably happening is that your cat is getting over stimulated. His particular response is to growl and hiss. HE may not think he's had enough but it would be wise of you to treat it as such and let him calm down. Give him some positive reinforcement when the game is over.

He would wake us up every morning scratching the door, and that would make me crazy for a long time, until I decided to buy a kid's water-gun, and spray him every time he would do that. After a week, I could sleep without problems.

I have used the same method to correct some some bad habits, but now I have come across one that I am uncertain how to approach it.

Sometimes, when I am tired and I lay on the bed, he comes next to me, and lays with his belly up, to be cuddled. But when he has had enough of it, instead of just going away, he scratches me. I would like to teach him a better way to communicate "I have had enough", but I am not sure how can I achieve such goal.

Does anyone has any idea?

That's how cats communicate "I've had enough". Watch your cat's body language throughout your petting session and you'll see it change from relaxed contentment to more tense and action-ready, up until the point that he scratches you.

Watch for signs like wide open, alert eyes, twitchy ears and whiskers, fidgety paws, and a lashing or thrashing tail. These might be endearing or cute to look at, but they're all very clear communications that your cat is getting perturbed. Keep your eyes out for these signs and stop petting when you notice them. It would be unfair to punish the cat for a reaction that you're causing by being inattentive.

Q: My cat buries his food. Why? Being a cat owner for many decades and knowing much about these enigmatic creatures, my new rescue kitten (about a year old), has the strangest behavior: After eating, he scratches the floor, multiple times, …
A: Some cats have a stronger burying instinct than others, and will scratch to bury at surfaces that are completely unsuitable to burying, sometimes even to only cover up a smell, as there is no physical object to bury.

My cat, for instance, is a enthusiastic bury-er that scratches at his litter, the sides of the box, around the outside of the box, and any nearby objects will end up in the box. He will do this sometimes even if he's not just used the box, but because he's so fastidious about burying. I've also seen him attempting to bury nowhere near his box, at nothing. Apparently a rogue smell is enough to make him want to bury.

Therefore, I have the impression that your cat still smells the food after it has eaten it, and is trying to cover up the smell by burying.

Q: My dog drank some beer someone left on the table during our party.
A: Alcohol is absorbed quickly and can be dangerous for pets. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Signs include vomiting, diarrhea, wobbling, sleepiness, trouble breathing and tremors, and in severe cases coma or death.

Before you go:
- Tell the vet what drink it was and roughly how much he had.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Don't give coffee or anything else to "sober him up". Caffeine is also toxic to pets.

On the way, keep him calm and watch his breathing.

Raw bread dough with yeast can also make alcohol inside the stomach, so keep both drinks and dough out of reach.

Q: In a multiple cat home, how many litter boxes should you have? I have seen a few suggestions in answers to other questions about it. But when I look I can never find it. If I have multiple cats in …
A: Rule of thumb is n + 1 litter boxes for n cats where n is greater than 1, this ensures a plentiful supply of this particular resource - with cats behaving more as individuals than a co-operative unit (such as a pack) they are more likely to accept sharing territory with another cat if there is no competition for key resources (toilet area, food, water etc)

It's by no means a hard and fast rule - my two get on just fine with two boxes between them but particularly during the introduction phase ensuring no or minimal resource competition is highly recommended.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

A: For a kitten this young you need to stimulate the kitten to poop and pee. This is very important to do and if you do not do this, the kitten is at risk of dying.

It is necessary to stimulate kittens of less than two weeks old to urinate and defecate as they cannot do this without stimulation from the mother cat. Where the mother is not available, urination and defecation must be maintained by the human carer for approximately four weeks or until the kitten is independent.

Q: How do I know if my old dog has arthritis?
A: Arthritis (joint wear and pain) is common in older dogs. Look for:
- Stiffness, especially after resting
- Limping or a changed way of walking
- Trouble with stairs, jumping into the car or onto the sofa, or getting up
- Less interest in walks or play
- Thinner leg muscles
- Grumpiness or snapping when touched

What helps:
- Keep your dog at a healthy weight
- Gentle, regular exercise like leash walks
- Non-slip rugs and ramps at home

See your vet for a proper diagnosis and pain plan. Don't give any pain medicine, including human medicine, without your vet's advice.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

Q: Dog howling at emergency response vehicles, is this normal? I have a 3-year-old Gerbian Shepsky who whenever he hears fire truck, ambulance, or police car sirens he just starts howling (he does not howl at car horns, but he will …
A: Many dogs howl at sirens, so it's nothing to be concerned about. There are a few reasons we think this happens, though experts aren't sure:
- To communicate with what they may think is another dog (The Spruce Pets)
- To alert you to an abnormal sound they think you should know about (Hill's)
- To scare the sound away, which in their mind may work because the siren does move away from them—this can in turn reinforce the behavior and make them do it more

Given that your dog reserves the howling for the sirens but barks at other loud things, it could be that either your dog perceives one as a threat but not the other, one as another dog howling and not the other, or something altogether different! While a normal behavior, it's still a mysterious one.

Q: Which causes more stress for a cat, losing its owner or moving? My grandma is moving into an assisted living facility. She currently lives on a 10 acre farm with her outdoor cat that's about 9 years old. A family …
A: Either situation will cause stress to the cat. The more important question should be: What is the best for the cat?

The answer depends on the personality of the cat.
- If he is used to roam the farm every day and goes stir crazy if confined to the farm house for a day, you should leave him at the farm.
- If the cat snuggles with your grandma or sleeps inside the house all day and doesn't care too much about going outside, move him in with grandma.
- If the cat roams the farm and is very affectionate, you should ask yourself: Is the new apartment big enough? Will he find enough entertainment to be happy? Most problematic behaviors in pets are caused by boredom. If your grandma cannot play with the cat anymore due to physical constraints, she might become overwhelmed if he develops problematic behaviors. The safest choice is to leave the cat at the farm.

Q: What container holds a 26-pound bag of kibble? I would like to transfer the contents of a 26-pound bag of dry dog food from the bag to a more convenient container. Any suggestions for a container to hold that amount, …
A: 7-Gallon Bucket

That 26-pound bag happens to just fit a 7-gallon bucket available from brewers supply companies with just a bit of room to spare.

Add a screw-type lid from a home building supply company and you have a nice complete kibble storage system.

Calculation

My clever friend determined this would work by weighing a cup of the kibble, and dividing that weight into the 26 pounds to determine how many cups of kibble are in a bag. The she divided the 7 gallon volume to get the number of cups would fit in the bucket. Voilà.

You could apply this strategy to your own kibble and your own container under consideration.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: My dog bit a big palaka (toad) in the yard and now he's foaming at the mouth.
A: Act fast. The big cane toad, now found on most Philippine islands, makes a venom that can affect the heart and nerves. Rinse his mouth, then go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Right away, if he is awake and alert:
- Rinse his mouth with running water for 5 to 10 minutes. Aim the water from the back of the mouth toward the front, with his head tilted down so it runs out. Don't let him swallow it.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

Serious signs can appear within 30 minutes to a few hours: vomiting, trembling, an irregular heartbeat, trouble breathing, bluish gums and seizures.

On the way, keep him calm, and take a photo of the toad if you can. Don't leave pet food or water outside, since it attracts toads.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

A: Animals (and humans btw) can distinguish materials and textures they lick. If your cat has a habit of grooming you, she knows how your skin or toe is supposed to feel. Q: A bee stung my dog and his face is swelling up.
A: Swelling of the face, head or neck after a sting can become serious because it can block breathing. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the swelling is large or spreading, if he has any trouble breathing, or if he was stung inside the mouth or on the tongue.

While you get ready to go:
- If you can see the stinger, scrape it out sideways with a flat card. Don't squeeze it with tweezers.
- Hold a cold pack wrapped in a cloth on the swollen spot.
- On the way, watch his breathing closely.

Don't give him any human allergy medicine unless your vet tells you to. Even if the swelling seems mild, call your vet for advice.

Q: Is psychology of the cat that has been raised by humans natural? I give food to the homeless cats around my house، To prevent their hunger One of them was a kitten؛ I was his/her only source of food، He/she …
A: A cat that from a very young age* has been raised by humans does have a different psychology than one that was raised by another cat. I have observed several cats who were raised this way and they tend to be more human focused than other cats. They may not interact completely normally with other cats, but can learn normal cat-like behavior over time if given enough exposure to other cats.

As far as violence between cats go, this is normal cat behavior. Normal cats can and do defend what they see as their territory from strange cats that trespass. A cats territory includes people and food in that territory as well.

(*Normally the 'very young age' is approximately around the time the kitten opens its eyes or younger. If a cat has any exposure to another cat (usually its mother) after this, it tends to have normal cat behavior.)

Q: What are the signs of tick fever in dogs?
A: "Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

Q: New cats are avoiding me So this woman lost her job and car and has become a semi-truck driver and didn't have a home for her two cats. So I rehomed them, but since they arrived four days ago, they …
A: It's very normal for cats to take a while to warm up to new people, spaces, or animals. Sometimes, cats take up to a year to get to know a new human, and their behavior towards you will continue to change while that happens.

Your new adopted cats probably don't think that you took them away from something, but they likely don't understand why the change has occurred or that they can trust you.

The best strategy is to be patient. Don't chase after them, let them come to you. Go about your daily business, and say hello to them when you see them. When you have a moment, sitting quietly on or near the floor will help them view you as less of a threat and they'll be more likely to approach.

This article has several pieces of excellent advice about acclimating new cats.

Good luck!

Q: Do I need to keep my dog's vaccination card?
A: Yes. Section 5 of RA 9482 requires owners to keep a registration card that records all of their dog's vaccinations. The implementing rules say the card should show the registration number, the dog's description, and vaccination details.

Keep it safe because you may need it:
- To show your dog is registered and vaccinated if asked by the LGU
- To get a BAI shipping permit when travelling with your pet
- If your dog bites someone and its rabies status is checked

Taking a photo of the card is a handy backup.

Q: Puppy eating food, covered with hair, problem? My puppy will sometimes refuse to eat his food and dump it in his crate. So every once in a while I'll pull out his tray and let him eat it. But as …
A: The short answer: No, very unlikely.

Remember wild carnivores (like wolves) will inevitable end up eating bits and pieces of their prey, including hair (and even bones). And don't forget about their own hair during cleaning.

Excessive amounts of hair can upset a dog's stomach (and theoretically even cause clogging), but these are typically vomited back out, if not at least partially digested.

Overall I'd say it's unlikely to cause any harm from your description. (How do you define "covered" here? 4-5 hairs?) If you still worry, occasionally add a few dips of (fish) oil to food you know the dog will eat without tossing around or storing (to avoid stains). Just keep in mind this might cause diarrhea, if you're adding too much. But on the plus side it will help with shedding and the fur's health overall.

If you think your dog is losing an excessive/too massive amount of hair, talk about it with your vet.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

Q: How is rabies spread?
A: Rabies spreads through the saliva of an infected animal, mostly through:

- Bites
- Scratches
- Saliva getting into open wounds, eyes, nose or mouth

Dogs cause up to 99% of human rabies cases worldwide, according to the WHO. In the Philippines, the DOH said 45% of rabies cases in 2024 came from the saliva of household pets.

Touching or feeding an animal, or a lick on unbroken skin, is not considered an exposure. Still, wash the area with soap and water.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

A: No, there is not a strictly internal/oral medication that can be used to treat maggots living in a live dog. The condition is called fly strike or Myiasis it can be fatal if untreated, there has been some success orally with Ivermectin in treating cattle, but there is some indication that dying larvae excrete toxins that can be fatal so close monitoring of the animal is required.

Most remedies involve physically removing the maggots, followed by treatment for related issues.

Q: How can we encourage our kitten to come up to us, if we're unable to get down on the floor with her? My brother just lost his cat to cancer, he is alone, and really needs companionship of our kitten. …
A: You mention you not being able to crawl, but are you able to just sit or lie on the floor, maybe propped up by a pillow? One way to convince a cat you're not a threat is to be in its space and then ignore it. The cat will eventually get bored and come out to investigate. However, the lower you are and the smaller you look, the less threatening you seem and the sooner their general fear will turn to boredom, hence why sitting or lying the floor (if you can do it) will work better than a chair or couch.

You can use that time to read a book, play games on your phone, talk softly, etc. Try not to approach the cat or make eye contact, loud noises or sudden large movements; they will interpret those things from strangers as possible threats and retreat/hide.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.
