Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: do i need to register my dog?
A: Yes. Under Section 5 of RA 9482 (Anti-Rabies Act of 2007), dog owners must submit their dogs for registration with the local government unit (LGU).

The implementing rules (Joint Administrative Order No. 1, s. 2008) say registration must be renewed every year. The LGU gives each registered and vaccinated dog a dog tag (Section 7).

Ask your city or municipal veterinary office or barangay where and when they register dogs. Spayed or neutered dogs get a discounted registration fee under Section 10.

Q: Is it ok to feed my cat one chicken liver daily? Is it ok to feed my cat [5 months] one chicken liver daily? I feed her as follows - 1 wing - 1 gizzard - 1 liver - 1 …
A: Do NOT feed your cat chicken liver daily.

Liver contains a lot of vitamin A, which is possible for cats to overdose on. This is called vitamin A toxicity. The toxicity will slowly build up over time, so consumption of foods very high in vitamin A should be limited overall, and not just limited to not eating too much in one meal.

Furthermore, I would be concerned that feeding your cat such a diet could lead to nutritional deficiencies, so unless you have done the research, it is just better to feed your cats catfood which has been proven to have the correct nutrition for cats.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: My dog is limping. What should I do?
A: Limping usually means pain or weakness, so it deserves a vet check.

First aid at home:
- Keep him calm and limit his activity.
- Gently check the paw for cuts, a broken nail, or something stuck between the toes. Stop if he shows pain. Dogs in pain may bite, even their owners.
- Don't give human pain medicines unless your vet tells you to. They can poison pets.

Go to the vet now if he:
- Won't put any weight on the leg, or the leg looks bent or swollen
- Can't stand or walk without help
- Was hit by a vehicle or attacked by another animal
- Is in severe pain, or the limp came on suddenly and badly

See your vet within 24 hours if the limp lasts more than a day or is getting worse. A short video of him walking at home helps the vet.

Q: Is it safe to let my cat walk on the roof?

I have a cat, who is 8 months old and occasionally climbs out the window to the roof. Is it safe to let my cat wander on the roof?
A: No it is not safe for cats to go out the window and on to the roof. The obvious first concern is falling.

If your cat did not fall to it's death the first time, it is unlikely to fall next time. The bigger risk is that there is no place to hide, and the cat is very visible from the sky. Birds of prey can be a risk to small pets your cat is at risk of being dinner for a bird of prey.

Additional risks include:
- Accidentally getting locked out, being subject to direct sunlight with no shade or water all day while you are away.
- Seeking shelter on the roof when sick or injured, creating great difficulty for you to provide care.

Q: How can I stop a cat from preventing another cat in the house from using the litter box? When going to work, two cats are left alone in the house. When coming home at night, there's a big mess on …
A: Add a second litter box to the house.

It is not unusual for any animal to get overly protective of 'their' litter box. I have seen this behavior in both cats and rabbits. It is generally solved by adding a second litter box some distance from the first. While the more aggressive pet might want to protect both boxes, it is logistically difficult to do so if they are well separated.

There are many variables, but either both pets will start sharing both boxes, or one pet will use one exclusively while the more dominant pet will use both. In either case, there will be adequate facilities available.

There may be other behavior issues that need to be addressed as well you can find related questions here

The next solution is to possibly make the more aggressive cat an outdoor cat, but that might not be fair. What can be done to curb bullying where one cat won't let the other cat use the litter box?

Add a second litter box to the house.

It is not unusual for any animal to get overly protective of 'their' litter box. I have seen this behavior in both cats and rabbits. It is generally solved by adding a second litter box some distance from the first. While the more aggressive pet might want to protect both boxes, it is logistically difficult to do so if they are well separated.

There are many variables, but either both pets will start sharing both boxes, or one pet will use one exclusively while the more dominant pet will use both. In either case, there will be adequate facilities available.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: My dog is limping. What should I do?
A: Limping usually means pain or weakness, so it deserves a vet check.

First aid at home:
- Keep him calm and limit his activity.
- Gently check the paw for cuts, a broken nail, or something stuck between the toes. Stop if he shows pain. Dogs in pain may bite, even their owners.
- Don't give human pain medicines unless your vet tells you to. They can poison pets.

Go to the vet now if he:
- Won't put any weight on the leg, or the leg looks bent or swollen
- Can't stand or walk without help
- Was hit by a vehicle or attacked by another animal
- Is in severe pain, or the limp came on suddenly and badly

See your vet within 24 hours if the limp lasts more than a day or is getting worse. A short video of him walking at home helps the vet.

Q: What should I keep in a first aid kit for my dog and cat?
A: A basic kit helps in the first minutes, but it never replaces a vet. Useful items:

- Gauze, sterile pads, stretch bandage and adhesive tape
- Small blunt-tipped scissors and tweezers
- Saline solution for rinsing wounds and eyes
- Cotton balls or swabs and disposable gloves
- A muzzle for dogs, and a towel for wrapping or carrying
- A rectal thermometer and lubricating jelly
- Splint material
- A small supply of your pet's regular medicines
- Your vet's number, the nearest 24-hour clinic, and your pet's health records

Keep it in a box with a secure lid you can grab fast, and check expiry dates every year. Ask your vet before giving any medicine, and only make your pet vomit if a vet tells you to. In an emergency, go to a vet now and use the kit on the way, not instead of going.

A: Your question can't really be answered canonically, but there are a few things you might do:

- Train a reliable recall that's strong enough that you can count on it in an emergency situation.
- Bring a soft-sided dog crate with you into your tent, and ensure the dog sleeps there.

Q: Do dogs seek revenge on their owners? Let's say a pet owner leave his dog inside for a whole day because of a trip. The owner returns to find that the dog has peed on the furniture. Is the dog …
A: Dogs do not have a concept of "revenge". Their mental processes revolve primarily around the "pack" identity: one member of the pack is the alpha, and all have their places in a distinct pecking order. (For owners that aren't mindful of this psychology, the dog usually believes itself to be the alpha.)

If your dog is fully housebroken, it probably held its bladder for as long as it could stand to (and likely experienced a feeling of failure when it couldn't hold it any longer).

If the dog's house training is not complete, then it should come as no surprise that it couldn't go all day.

Q: My dog ate rat poison from under the sink but he's acting normal.
A: Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, even though he seems fine. Many rat poisons stop the blood from clotting, and bleeding may not show right away. Early treatment gives the best chance of recovery.

Signs to watch for: low energy, not eating, weakness, pale gums, fast breathing, nosebleeds, and blood in the urine, stool or eyes.

Before you go:
- Bring the package or a photo of the label. Rat poisons work in different ways and need different treatment.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Check whether other pets could have eaten some.

On the way, handle him gently and keep him calm. Dogs and cats can also be poisoned by eating a poisoned rat, so tell the vet if that's possible.

Q: Is it OK to feed dogs dairy products? A recent answer included feeding dairy products to a dog, in the answer is was Cream Cheese, but it does bring up the whole question of if dairy products are appropriate for …
A: It probably comes as a surprise to most people, but many adult dogs and cats are actually lactose intolerant as well. While they may enjoy the taste of dairy, it's not a normal part of either diet and can lead to:
- Flatulence
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting

It doesn't take much either, according to Blackwell, 1.5 grams per kilogram of lactose per day can cause these symptoms and, for reference, 1 cup of milk has about 11 grams of lactose in it. So, unless there's a specific need to feed them dairy (e.g. illness recovery on recommendation of a vet), I would probably avoid it.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Q: Does my dog really need the lepto vaccine?
A: Leptospirosis is a serious bacterial disease that can also infect people. Dogs and rats can carry it and pass it out in their urine. The germs can survive for weeks to months in water and soil, and the risk goes up after floods and heavy rain.

The 2024 WSAVA guidelines say all dogs should be vaccinated where leptospirosis occurs and suitable vaccines are available.

In general:
- The first course is two doses given 2 to 4 weeks apart
- After that, a booster is usually needed every year

Keep your dog out of floodwater and puddles when you can. Your vet will tell you if lepto vaccine is right for your dog and when to give it.

Q: Is some blood during cat delivery normal?

A: Some fluid isn't abnormal, there will be a small amount at the start as she discharges the vaginal plug prior to birthing the first kitten. During the process, she will chew off the umbilical cords of each kitten. Finally, as her uterus contracts there will be some additional fluid discharged.

Observation, post delivery, is important though. If you continue to see a bright, red, bloody discharge continue or she shows signs of disinterest or lethargy, unwillingness to eat, then it may be wise to contact a vet for advice. Don't stress though, cats have been doing this for thousands of years without our help. :)

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: Can cats get heartworm?
A: Yes. Cats get heartworm the same way dogs do, from mosquito bites, and indoor cats can be bitten too.

Signs can be mild or sudden:
- Coughing or asthma-like breathing attacks
- Vomiting, poor appetite, weight loss
- Trouble walking, fainting or seizures

Sometimes the first sign is sudden collapse. See a vet now if your cat has trouble breathing or collapses.

There is no approved medicine to cure heartworm in cats, and the dog treatment is not safe for them. That makes prevention the only real protection. Ask your vet for a heartworm preventive made for cats that suits your cat's weight and age.

Q: My old pet has really bad breath. Is that dental disease?
A: Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Q: Will playing near undesirable pee location dissuade future soiling? My cat has peed on the sofa. Will playing with her at/near the sofa reinforce or prevent her from choosing that location again for peeing? My intuition is that if she …

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: My old cat drinks a lot of water and pees a lot. Why?
A: Drinking and peeing more is a common early sign of kidney disease in older cats. Kidney disease affects up to 40% of cats over 10 and about 80% of cats over 15.

Other signs can follow:
- Weight loss
- Poor appetite
- Low energy and a messy coat

The same signs can also come from diabetes or an overactive thyroid, so blood and urine tests are needed to find the cause.

Book a vet visit soon, and don't limit her water. Go to a vet today if she stops eating, vomits repeatedly or seems very weak. Catching kidney disease early, often with a special diet, can help your cat feel better for longer.

Q: Can rabies be cured?
A: Once symptoms show, rabies is almost always fatal, in both people and animals. That's why acting before symptoms appear is so important.

Rabies is fully preventable:
- After a bite or scratch, wash the wound well and get post-exposure prophylaxis at an Animal Bite Treatment Center right away
- Vaccinate your dogs and cats every year

In people, symptoms can appear about one week to one year after exposure, usually after 2 to 3 months. So don't wait to see if you feel sick.

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

A: It is indeed a moan and is part of the natural range of vocalizations a dog uses.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: How do I know if my cat has worms? Are there any specific signs my cat will show if he has worms? I know that horses can get diarrhea, loose weight or don't gain weight and that you can detect …
A: Yes, there are general signs related to their stool as you noted, including diarrhea, blood, or constipation. For other signs, you should be looking for:
- Unexplained weight loss
- Vomiting
- Coughing and other breathing difficulties

In general, though, being able to see them poop (or the outcome of it) is the most effective way to detect the presence of certain worms as not all symptoms may apply to varieties of worms. For example, the stool is important for detecting roundworms and hookworms. The weight loss and vomiting would more likely signal a tapeworm and coughing/breathing issues for lungworm.

If you're really concerned, take him into the vet for an examination. The risk is higher for outdoor cats who are more likely to be exposed to fleas and other parasites.

Q: How can I remove multiple ticks from a dog quickly? There's a female stray dog in my area who was recently spayed and as being spayed in a poor Indian government hospital she's got ticks all over her body. Manual …
A: Manual removal is best, because it also allows you to clean/disinfect the wounds with isopropyl alcohol (or other disinfectant). If she doesn't sit still for you to remove all of the ticks at once, you can try just pulling off one or two at a time, then giving her a break (petting her, giving her treats, playing a game, etc) before pulling off another tick or two.

You can use some sprays or medications (many of them are found in these charts), but they can be dangerous if the dog is exposed to them multiple times in a single month. For example, if you treat her and then tomorrow your neighbor treats her because your neighbor didn't know that you already sprayed her. She may get an overdose and become very ill. You should read the directions and make sure that the product that you chose can be applied frequently without any danger.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: What is a hound?

It is a truism that all hounds are dogs, but that not all dogs are hounds. What makes a hound, well, a hound? Is it genetic, ability, purpose, or all three?
A: A hound is a type of dog breed that was originally used for hunting due to its scenting (Beagle, Basset or Bloodhound) or sighting (Afghan Hound, Greyhound or Whippet) abilities.

To be more precise, here's the definition of the hound group from the AKC:

Most hounds share the common ancestral trait of being used for hunting. Some use acute scenting powers to follow a trail. Others demonstrate a phenomenal gift of stamina as they relentlessly run down quarry. Beyond this, however, generalizations about hounds are hard to come by, since the Group encompasses quite a diverse lot. There are Pharaoh Hounds, Norwegian Elkhounds, Afghans and Beagles, among others. Some hounds share the distinct ability to produce a unique sound known as baying.

Other national kennel clubs have a similar definition, according to Wikipedia.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

When at home, your dog is in his territory and is just responding to what he believes is an outside intruder coming into his territory. This is why your dog immediately responded in the second case as soon as entered his yard.

Now is this normal? I wouldn't say it is abnormal, but if you dog will attack anyone (or at least any dog) that enters his yard, then that is something that needs dealt with because he could possible seriously injure someone (or some dog) who just happens to come into you yard.

Q: Can dogs get bored of a walk? I take my four-month-old puppy on about three walks per day. The walks are almost always a 15-20 minute loop starting at my house. It goes through several neighborhoods, a park, and on …
A: Without being able to cite any sources, the general answer is no.

I've heard that many dogs enjoy walking the same path every day, because
- It gives them a routine and they know what to expect. Especially anxious dogs feel safer when they can predict what's going to happen.
- Dogs have much more sensory input than humans. For example, they smell who was there since the last time. That makes the same old path less boring for them.
- Wild dogs would patrol the borders of their territory in regular intervals. Taking the same walk every day might feel like that for your dog.

That being said, there's also nothing wrong with changing routes and exploring new paths every day. You just don't have to if you don't want to.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: Should I carry my elderly cocker spaniel out of the car? I own a 13 year old cocker spaniel. I like to drive him around in my 2002 Toyota highlander. I'm worried though, because he has to jump about 2-3 …
A: We kept large dogs (GSDs and Labs) for many years. All of them became arthritic in their old age, and getting in and out of vehicles could be a problem. Some of the dogs didn't mind being lifted in and out, but others found that to be painful, especially if you caught a hip joint awkwardly. The solution was simple enough: a ramp made out of a piece of plywood with some carpet glued on for traction. This allowed the dog to get in an out of a vehicle in its own time, and without the risk of being inexpertly handled. You can buy pet ramps if you do not want to make your own, although a box large enough to act as a step may be all that is needed.

Q: How often should I deworm my puppy?
A: Puppies pick up worms easily, so they're dewormed more often than adults. A common schedule is:
- Every 2 weeks from about 2 weeks old until 12 weeks
- Then monthly until 6 months old
- Then every 3 months for adults

Your vet will choose the right product and dose for your puppy's weight, so ask them before giving anything. Keep the yard clean and treat fleas too, since fleas can spread tapeworm.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

A: Best suggestion I've got:

Re-introduce yourself as you would to a Dog you've never seen before and that isn't sure it trusts you.Go outside, sit down, and give her a chance to come to you, with lots of space to retreat so she doesn't feel threatened. Q: Small dog is scared of my cat My cat attacked my sons small dog when he was a puppy. I am now living with my son and his little dog is terrified of my cat. How can I get them …
A: You should show him that nothing bad happens when he's close to the cat. One approach that worked well for me was to sit down with the scared animal (in your case the dog) and pet it. Then call the second animal to you and pet both at the same time.

Make sure you have each animal on either side of you. You are the safety wall that makes your dog feel protected while that cat is near.

This won't change things over night. You have to repeat the procedure every day to let your dog learn to not be afraid. Over time, you can make them come closer to each other.

Your dog might never feel comfortable playing with or snuggling up to your cat. You should respect that. But your dog shouldn't feel afraid in his own home.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: Why does my dog howl at airplanes? I noticed that whenever an airplane passes over our house, my dog starts howling and doesn't stop until the plane is a very far distance from our house. Is this a normal behaviour? …
A: In addition to John Cavan's answer, if you've ruled out any medical problems your dog most likely howls at the plane to make it go away - and it's working!

If planes pass over your house frequently enough, you'll want to desensitise your dog to the noise.

Try searching for airplane noises on YouTube and play them at a volume that your dog is comfortable with. Reward with lots of treats and praise.

Increase the volume in very small steps, as you will undo a lot of the work if you misjudge your dog's limits and he starts howling.

Have lots of patience, it'll likely take a while for your dog to get used to the noise and to associate it with good things happening(TM).

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: My dog licked toilet bowl cleaner and my cat stepped in spilled bleach. What do I do?
A: Strong cleaners can burn the mouth, throat, skin and eyes. Burns from drain cleaners may not hurt at first and can show up hours later. Cats often lick chemicals off their paws. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and go in.

Before and on the way:
- Don't make your pet vomit. It can cause more burns.
- Ask the vet before giving anything to drink. They may tell you to offer water or milk.
- Rinse skin and paws with lots of water, then wash with mild shampoo.
- If it got in the eyes, flush with water or saline for a long time, ideally while someone else drives.
- Move your pet to fresh air if there are fumes.
- Bring the bottle.

Never mix bleach with ammonia cleaners, as this makes a toxic gas.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: Do we really know if cats are "playing"? So I have a new kitten (8 weeks). She's adorable as anything but she engages in a lot of "play" fighting (scratching, pawing, biting, pouncing, etc). It doesn't bother me at all …
A: Play is almost universal among animals with large enough brains to react/interact creatively with their siblings and surroundings. It is far from being specific to humans, and not limited to juveniles. Zoos have learned that providing "enrichment activities" for animals makes them happier, healthier, and less frustrated.

At its base, play is enjoyment in practicing skills that the animal needs. Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: My dog is limping. What should I do?
A: Limping usually means pain or weakness, so it deserves a vet check.

First aid at home:
- Keep him calm and limit his activity.
- Gently check the paw for cuts, a broken nail, or something stuck between the toes. Stop if he shows pain. Dogs in pain may bite, even their owners.
- Don't give human pain medicines unless your vet tells you to. They can poison pets.

Go to the vet now if he:
- Won't put any weight on the leg, or the leg looks bent or swollen
- Can't stand or walk without help
- Was hit by a vehicle or attacked by another animal
- Is in severe pain, or the limp came on suddenly and badly

See your vet within 24 hours if the limp lasts more than a day or is getting worse. A short video of him walking at home helps the vet.

Q: Does my dog need boots for winter? Winter will be early in my country this year. I have Labrador that is going to be one year old by then. And during extreme cold, temperature may fall below 10 degrees Celsius, …
A: Have you ever seen wolves hunt in the snow wearing their winter boots?

So the short answer is: No, unless there's a specific medical condition you don't.

Make sure the dog has a warm place to stay in rather than stand/sit on the cold floor all the time and you should be fine.

Far more important, depending on where you live, is cleaning the paws from salt (water) from roads as that can cause irritation or other issues (e.g. when licked on). Ideally this should happen after every walk, just using some warm water should be enough.

You can also buy special wax or sprays to better seal/protect the paws, but that's really optional, especially if your dog is not working (e.g. sled pulling).

A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Apply direct pressure with a (non-adhesive) gauze pad until the bleeding is completely stopped.

As always, when in doubt- vet.

She knows what I want her to do, just refuses to obey. Other commands are fine.

Take it slow and start from square one to regain her trust and confidence. Get her to associate finger and "bang" with good feelings by playing with her affectionately (petting, calm approval voice, gentle and slow) and presenting that stimulus until it is no longer associated with the physical pain.

Q: Which home made foods/meals can dog eat?

I don't want to buy packaged dog foods. What meals i can offer for him? E.g spaghetti, bread, milk? I mean not specially prepared food but foods that human eats.
A: You shouldn't make your own dog food without learning what dogs need in their daily diet first.

None of your suggestions are healthy dog food. Especially the salt and spices in human food are unhealthy for dogs. There are very common ingredients in human food that are harmful or even poisonous for dogs. You would cause malnutrition and illnesses in your dog if you fed him like that every day.

There are some recipes floating around the internet on how to make dog food at home, but I will not point you to any of them, because:
- It's very easy to make mistakes, leading to either a deficit of vital components or an excess of unhealthy components.
- Making healthy meals for a dog is just as expensive as buying dog food, because you need to feed lots of meat.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

The genetics of catnip susceptibility

In doing a little looking around, I found three different answers to the question: What percent of cats are susceptible to catnip?
- The Humane Society says "an estimated 50 percent"
- Scientific American says "about 70 to 80 percent"
- Cat World says "around 50–66%"

Each source carefully notes the figure as an estimate. None of them cite any sources or give any explanation beyond the figures coming from "experts." (You'd think someone would take a poll, but that's not my point)

I recall hearing many years ago that the gene for catnip sensitivity followed a simple dominant-recessive pattern. Similar to Mendel's peas, in a well-mixed population, you'll have the pairs RR, Rr, rR, and rr - only 25% (the rr group) will not express the trait, the other 75% will. That would lend support to Scientific American's numbers.

However, if the genes that cause catnip sensitivity exhibit some form of co-dominance, like human blood groups, then the percentages can skew.

So my question comes down to: What hard-science exists to explain the variation in sensitivity to catnip among cats? Have there been any long-term breeding experiments? Has that portion of the feline genome been explored at all?
I couldn't find this in FurFriends' checked sources, so I don't want to guess. Please ask your vet, and if your pet seems unwell or in pain, see them soon.

Q: How vulnerable are crossbred (hybrid) dogs to genetic disease? Most purebred dogs are prone to breed-specific diseases, for example, hip dysplasia in Labrador Retrievers. Mixed-breed (mongrel) dogs are said to be less prone to genetic diseases than purebred dogs due …
A: I'm going to interpret the genetics portion of the Wikipedia article you cited in plain English, and add what I know from college Biology class:

It depends on the parents you use.

Crossbreeding dogs (hybridization) is a tactic used by breeders to reduce the chance of inheriting a poor trait from a parent. Before breeding, it is important to already know the chance of disease for the particular source breed, and knowing the disease / genetic history of the individual source parent. Genetic testing of the parents prior to breeding may help disqualify parents for crossbreeding.

As a bastardization of theory, inbreeding has traditionally shown to produce poor genetic results; while the introduction of additional genes through cross-breeding may introduce different traits to a line, based on the rules of evolution, the resulting crossbred dog most likely to survive will be the one with the best genes.

Q: Can cats occasionally be fed rice? My children fed our cat a snack 1 of cooked white rice and tuna. Is it healthy for my cat to eat rice? 1 In Australia, by snack, I do not mean a treat, …
A: Sure you can feed them rice... but it isn't great for them. They are obligate carnivores meaning they must eat meat / poultry. Even if you specially processed vegetables to give them the correct caloric balance (fat / protein / carbs) they would die prematurely because they cannot fully convert things into the form they need (for instance taking the vegetable fats and converting them into the many things a body uses fat for, such as nerve insulation, cell walls,...).

Rice is not hideously poisonous to them (the high level of nitrates probably aren't great for them though) but it has a skewed caloric balance and is deficient in many areas. Rice is also a common "filler" in many cat foods especially dry foods (large amounts of vegetable matter in a cat food is a bad sign).

A: Balloon material cannot be digested by cats. It may be able to pass through her digestive system, but it may also cause a blockage. A blockage is a VERY SERIOUS problem that requires IMMEDIATE vet attention.

Symptoms of a blockage can include:
- Vomiting
- Anorexia (not eating)
- Weakness/lethargy
- Diarrhea
- Weight loss

If your cat exhibits any of these signs, you should take her to the vet immediately.

In the future, do not allow your cat to play with balloons (or if you do, clip her claws beforehand and supervise her closely while she has access to the balloon).

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: A dog bit me (nakagat ako ng aso). What should I do?
A: Act right away, even if the dog looks healthy.

- Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
- Don't put garlic or other home remedies on it, and don't rely on "tandok" or "tambal" healers
- Go to the nearest Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) or Animal Bite Center promptly for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
- Finish the full vaccine schedule the health workers give you

Don't wait for symptoms. Once rabies symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. If the dog has an owner, they should report the bite and have the dog observed for 14 days.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: How do I safely move an injured dog or cat to the vet?
A: Call your vet first, then leave as soon as you can. To move your pet safely:

- Protect yourself. Pain can make any pet bite or scratch. Covering the head and eyes with a towel can calm them.
- A cloth muzzle can help with dogs, but don't use one on flat-faced breeds or a dog with a chest injury, and never leave a muzzled dog alone.
- Keep the head, neck and spine as still as possible. Use a board, thick cardboard or a folded blanket as a stretcher.
- Put cats and small pets in a box or carrier with air holes.
- If something is stuck in the body, don't pull it out. Keep it from moving.
- Move slowly and avoid sudden jerks.

On the way, have one person drive while another watches the pet.

When this happens her flight response kicks in and she wants to take off running. She's securely on leash and won't get away, but I often will just start running with her. She also likes to run, more often when she's off-leash at the dog park or the beach, so it's not something she only does when she's scared. I partially hope that by running with her when she's scared she might forget she's scared and just be happy running.

How do I discourage my cat from biting?

I adopted an adult cat from a shelter. The cat had been seized (along with 20+ others) by Animal Control from a hoarder and there is no prior medical history. Age estimates range from 3-6 years and he was one of the older ones in the group. He had already been neutered when the shelter got him. Because of the circumstances we have no other pre-shelter history.

The cat gets along well with the people and other cat in the house, but sometimes he randomly "nips" (both people and the other cat), sometimes during play but sometimes just out of the blue. These nips are not hard enough to leave marks or draw blood, but it's still behavior that I would like to discourage. Hissing at him doesn't make any difference, and I don't always have a squirt bottle to hand. Years ago I had a kitten with this problem and was advised to hold his mouth shut and blow in his face to stop it; that worked on the kitten but has had no effect on the adult cat.

What techniques have others found effective in solving this problem?

I have not observed any territorial behavior (spraying) or true aggression.

Q: My German Shepherd ate a big meal and then ran around. Now he's restless and drooling. Can bloat wait until morning?
A: No. Bloat (GDV), where the stomach fills with gas and can twist, is a life-threatening emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now. Quick treatment greatly improves the chance of survival.

Signs to watch for:
- Restlessness and seeming uncomfortable
- Retching again and again with nothing coming up
- Lots of drooling
- A swollen, painful belly
- Fast breathing, pale gums, weakness

Large, deep-chested breeds like German Shepherds, Great Danes and Dobermans are at higher risk, especially when a big meal is followed by exercise.

On the way, keep him calm, don't give food or a lot of water, and call the clinic ahead so they can prepare.

Q: My dog is losing hair and very itchy. Is it mange?
A: Mange is caused by tiny mites. Dogs get two main types:

Sarcoptic mange (scabies):
- Sudden, intense itching
- Bumps and crusts, often on the belly, chest, ears, elbows and legs
- Very contagious to other dogs, and can cause itchy skin in people

Demodectic mange (demodex):
- Bald, red, scaly patches, often with little itching
- Common in young dogs; mild cases may clear on their own
- The widespread form needs vet treatment

Your vet will usually do a skin scraping to check. Treat all pets that have contact with each other at the same time, and clean bedding and grooming tools. Follow your vet's treatment plan, which can take a while.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: How do I keep my cat cool during hot days?
A: Cats handle heat better than many dogs, but hot, humid days can still be dangerous.
- Keep fresh water in several places, and add wet food for extra fluids
- Give them a shaded, airy spot, and use a fan or air-con in the hottest hours
- Brush long-haired cats often to remove loose fur
- Never leave a cat in a parked car

Open-mouth panting, drooling, wobbliness or collapse can mean heatstroke. Move them somewhere cool and go to a vet now.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: What papers do I need to bring my dog or cat to another island or province?
A: You need a local shipping permit from the Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), applied for online at nvqsd.bai.gov.ph. Under the BAI Citizen's Charter, dogs and cats need:

- A veterinary health certificate from a licensed vet, showing rabies vaccine details (brand, batch/lot number, date given, next due date)
- A rabies vaccination certificate signed by the vet with their PRC number
- The pet should be about 3 to 4 months old or older
- The rabies shot should be at least 14 days and not more than 1 year old (annual boosters can ship right away)

messages.content: What papers do I need to bring my dog or cat to another island or province?

You need a local shipping permit from the Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), applied for online at nvqsd.bai.gov.ph. Under the BAI Citizen's Charter, dogs and cats need:

- A veterinary health certificate from a licensed vet, showing rabies vaccine details (brand, batch/lot number, date given, next due date)
- A rabies vaccination certificate signed by the vet with their PRC number
- The pet should be about 3 to 4 months old or older
- The rabies shot should be at least 14 days and not more than 1 year old (annual boosters can ship right away)

The permit is free; processing takes up to 3 working days. Rules may change, so confirm with BAI before your trip.

Q: My pet seems sleepy after her shots. Normal or not?
A: Mild reactions are common and should be short-lived:
- Soreness or a small swelling where the shot was given
- Tiredness or less appetite
- Mild fever
- Vomiting once

Allergic reactions are less common but can be serious. Severe ones usually start within minutes to an hour, but other reactions can appear hours later. Go to a vet now if you see:
- Swelling of the face, lips or eyes
- Hives (raised bumps on the skin)
- Repeated vomiting or diarrhea
- Trouble breathing
- Weakness or collapse

Call your vet if mild signs do not improve or you are unsure. Always tell your vet about any past reaction before the next vaccine.

Q: Could my dog get infected with SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus and suffer from COVID-19?

I have heard, that dogs too could get the actual coronavirus. Is this real?
A: Coronaviruses are a large group of viruses, that most animals deals with every day without signs of illness.

The "new" coronavirus called "SARS-CoV-2" causing risk for health in humans, causes nearly no health issues in dogs.

But there are two other ("older") coronaviruses, that infects dogs with signs of illness, mainly diarrhoea. These viruses have no effect on the human health.

Additonal: in science there are two dogs noted, that were infected by SARS-CoV-2. Both cases occurred in Hongkong (very high COVID-19 density) and parts of the virus were found at the blood of both animals. But both cases had NO infectious (means whole, functional) virus in their body.

Source is the website of German Dog Association (VDH) publishing an interview with the director of the institute for animal hygiene and veterinarian association at the university of Leipzig.

Q: Can a cat with a sluggish colon have dry food? The is question Is there anything beyond preference that dictates whether dry food should be wet down? and comments brought up and interesting issue. If a cat has a sluggish …
A: Another issue you might want to consider is that as cats get older their colon response gets weaker.

My old (18.5 years) cat scared the living daylights out of me a couple of years back when one of her scent glands burst - in domestic cats the glands are usually emptied when the cat defecates, so anything that slows the process or causes a day or two of constipation increases the risk of a blockage (Diarrhea can also cause scent gland issues because the cat isn't having to push).

You'll probably need to adjust the cat's diet as she ages to keep her stool texture and frequency consistent, both for her comfort and to prevent scent gland problems.

Q: My male cat keeps crying in the litter box and licking his private area. Can it wait until tomorrow?
A: Please don't wait. A male cat that strains and passes little or no urine may have a blocked urethra. This is an absolute emergency. When urine can't get out, toxins build up quickly, and a blocked cat can die in less than a day or two.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

Other signs include blood in the urine, peeing outside the box, frequent trips to the box, and becoming more and more distressed.

On the way:
- Place him gently in a carrier and don't squeeze his belly.
- Keep him calm and quiet.
- Tell the clinic it's a male cat who can't pee, so they can be ready.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Attention and play are separate, one can give one's cat lots of love and attention and the cat might still want an outlet for its play behavior. A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

Q: From what height a cat can fall safely? There is a belief prevalent that cats can land on their paws harmlessly irrespective of the height. Assuming that the land below is plain soil, what can maximum if cat is drooped, …
A: There's a great term called "feline high-rise syndrome".

Roughly speaking, 90% of cats survive falls from 2-32 stories (approx 5-160 meters).

A Straight Dope article from 1996 conjectured that higher falls give the cat time to rotate (feet-down) and then relax, which causes their excess of skin to act somewhat like a parachute. Specifically, the article says that falls over seven stories are more survivable.

The 2004 Vnuk article specifically disputes this, stating:

Falls from the seventh or higher stories, are associated with more severe injuries and with a higher incidence of thoracic trauma.

The article also indicates a 96.5% survival rate, though half of those sustained limb fractures.

Incidentally, a physics.stackoverflow article says a "righted and relaxed" cat has a terminal velocity around 100kph, while reddit estimates a human's TV is about 160kph at the slowest (flat, stretched out).

Q: How often does my dog need the anti-rabies shot by law?
A: Every year. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must have their dogs "regularly" vaccinated against rabies. The implementing rules make it clearer: a properly immunized dog is one vaccinated yearly, and LGUs register and vaccinate dogs annually.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: Should you pet a bird, and if so, how?

Do birds respond to petting, like cats and dogs do? Do they like being gently brushed against their heads? Does grooming in this sense exist in the avian world?
A: Many socialized birds do enjoy a gently scratching. The favorite places are the side of the neck and some birds enjoy under the wing.

Many parrots do groom each other, especially areas they cannot reach themselves, like the back of the neck and head. Scratching these areas closely mimics this grooming. An important part of the grooming is to clean away the 'plastic like' casing around a new feather as it emerges.

A bird will give clear indication when they like it, often dropping their head and fluffing the feathers around the head and neck. Start slowly and gently until your bird grows accustomed to it. Every bird is different, some LOVE it and others do not. It is highly dependent on the bond you have developed with the bird.

A: He is doing this because dogs are curious and like eating things that are not dog food.

You can train your dog to avoid that but he'd still have to be very close to you even off-leash for supervision. Some dogs are extremely tempted by food and it's a hard behavior to break especially if your dog isn't trained.

In a controlled environment put small treats on the ground and let your dog off the leash slowly. Every time he approaches a treat on the ground give him a firm "No", when the dog does not eat them or loses interest in them reward him with a bigger treat. Repeat this exercise with bigger treats on the ground and longer distance.

This can take a while and success requires determination.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: How long should neutered cat use shredded newspaper litter box? I neutered my cat yesterday and changed his litter box so that it's full of shredded newspaper. For how long should he stay away from his regular sand litter box? …
A: Newspaper as a substitute for litter after neutering is a short-term approach. According to PetMD:

Sometimes litter can get stuck to the incision, so veterinarians will often recommend using torn newspaper in the litter box for 24 hours after surgery to avoid this.

Other sites recommend different periods; the Toby Project suggests five days, and SNAP recommends 7-10 days, but all cite the same reason of preventing litter dust from irritating or becoming embedded in the incisions.

Once the surgical incisions have closed up sufficiently that dust and particles of litter won't get stuck to them or cause irritation leading to pain or over-grooming, you should be safe to switch back to your regular litter.

Q: My dog chewed up a whole pack of sugar-free gum.
A: Take him to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, even if he looks fine. Many sugar-free gums contain xylitol (also called birch sugar), which can make a dog's blood sugar crash within 10 to 60 minutes. It can also harm the liver a day or two later, so he may need to stay for monitoring.

Watch for vomiting, weakness, wobbling, collapse and seizures.

Before you go:
- Bring the pack so the vet can check the ingredients.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him close, watch for weakness or shaking, and call the clinic ahead.

Xylitol is also in some peanut butters, toothpastes, mouthwashes and vitamins, so check labels and use only pet toothpaste.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: What should I do with a dog who is afraid of everyone except me? My dog is scared of everyone except me. He used to stay on a farm where some people always teased him. Now he is scared of …
A: You work on it slowly. Trust is a difficult thing. Take him out, slowly get him socialised to a few people, and more and more. Deal with how he manifests the fear - talking to a dog calmly and quietly works wonders.

You'll also have to use what motivates him to open up. Once he realises that people have food/will play with him/will pet him, he'll start getting used to it. That said, some dogs are just not people dogs. Even if your dog isn't the center of attention, and ignores people, its better than fear ;).

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

A: I have seen several dogs that move while defecating, but never one that turns in tight circles. This seems to be some kind of natural behavior, so instead of trying to teach her to stay in one spot, teach her to move forward rather then in circles.

Keep her on leash, stay in front of her with no slack in the leash, not pulling, but just making forward the only choice. Praise her staying put as well as for moving forward. I would not use negative commands for turning, as you point out that only confuses her.

Q: My dog is limping. What should I do?
A: Limping usually means pain or weakness, so it deserves a vet check.

First aid at home:
- Keep him calm and limit his activity.
- Gently check the paw for cuts, a broken nail, or something stuck between the toes. Stop if he shows pain. Dogs in pain may bite, even their owners.
- Don't give human pain medicines unless your vet tells you to. They can poison pets.

Go to the vet now if he:
- Won't put any weight on the leg, or the leg looks bent or swollen
- Can't stand or walk without help
- Was hit by a vehicle or attacked by another animal
- Is in severe pain, or the limp came on suddenly and badly

See your vet within 24 hours if the limp lasts more than a day or is getting worse. A short video of him walking at home helps the vet.
