Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

A: Older dogs still need daily activity to keep their muscles, joints, weight and mind healthy. The type matters more than the amount:
- Choose gentle, low-impact exercise like shorter, more frequent leash walks or swimming
- Avoid lots of hard jumping and rough play
- Add brain games, new toys and simple training to keep the mind sharp

Q: What are the causes of a cat jumping off a roof?

Currently my cat is in serious condition and I was wondering: what happens if a cat fell from a high height, aka a roof?
A: Lots of things can make a cat fall/jump of a roof.
- Getting scared.
- Hunting attempts, for example trying to catch a bird.
- Overestimating his/her abilities.
- Getting distracted.

Cats can get hurt if the fall is too short, because they haven't enough time to righten themselves.

A cat can get hurt if it is overweight and it falls from great height.

Wanting to get down but landing wrong can cause injuries, this is most common in kittens and very young cats.

Additional information: often cats that fall from tall buildings have a greater survival rate and less injuries than cats falling from lower buildings.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

Q: Is it possible to overbrush a cat? I am taking care of an elderly Maine Coon who can't really groom himself well. He enjoys being brushed and he changes his lying position to indicate where he wants to get brushed. …
A: Actually, yes, it is possible to overbrush cats, though it also depends on what kind of brush you are using. The Furminator, for example, actually tends to pull out hair (which mind you doesn't hurt cats like it does humans), but it can actually thin out a cat's fur if used too much. If you use a more regular kind of brush that doesn't happen so much, and so it's probably fine to use on a regular basis. If you're really concerned, try to make sure you don't brush one area over and over, and keep an eye on your cat's fur.

Q: Can you bottle feed a kitten? I have an orphaned baby kitten and it is to young for solid food, how do I nurse them? The related question Kitten Food in an Emergency talks about what foods to use, but …
A: Yes, you can bottle-feed a kitten. There are kits designed for this purpose, available at many pet stores, but you don't necessarily need them if you have baby bottles at home. Basically, the key is to have the liquid be able to drip from the opening of the bottle slowly, without needing to squeeze it, so that the kitten can easily get the fluid without the need for significant suction. If you have a bottle that isn't doing that, you can widen the hole of the nipple using a heated needle.

As for milk, it's not cow's milk that you should be looking at. There are kitten milk replacements that you should get from the pet store or your vet. Warm this according to directions (about 100 °F / 37 °C) to avoid upset tummies.

Q: What is the minimum safe room temperature for puppies? My puppy is four months old. What is the minimum room temperature that he is comfortable? I plan to set the room temperature to 68 °F (20 °C) at nights. Is …
A: At 4 months of age a puppy can regulate their own body temperature well enough. Any temperature that's appropriate for an adult dog of that breed is also appropriate for the puppy. That mostly depends on the thickness of the fur and the body size, but even small dogs with thin fur have no problem with temperatures around 20°C.

Puppies cannot regulate their body temperature for the first 4 weeks of their life and may need an additional heat source if the mother is away. After that time, a room temperature between 20°C / 69°F (winter) and 26°C / 78°F (summer) is recommended (Source).

In my personal oppinion the lower (winter) temperature only has to be so high for hairless or very small dogs. Dogs with thicker fur (I'm thinking any sheepdog, retriever or terrier) should be fine with lower temperatures, especially if you give them a warm or insulating place to sleep.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

A: The best solution to your problem is to get a good scratching post for your cats.

If you get a scratching post for your cats, they likely will not use your sofa at all to sharpen their claws.

A god scratching post needs to be heavy so your cat is not able to move it. This means it must weigh 15-20 kilos or more. The scratching surface must be made of sisal or hemp rope so your cat can use its full strength when scratching.

One single cat claw can hold the cat's weight, so they are strong.

For your cats sitting on the sofa, you can use a folded towel for them to lie/sit on.

Q: My dog was panting really hard after our walk in the heat and now he collapsed. What do I do?
A: This sounds like heatstroke, which is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

Before you leave and on the way:
- Move him out of the sun into shade or an air-conditioned space.
- Wet his body with cool (not ice-cold) water or wet towels, especially the belly, and use a fan or the car aircon.
- Don't dunk him in a tub of cold water.
- Offer small sips of water only once he is alert and starting to cool.

Other heatstroke signs are hot skin, drooling, vomiting, and wobbly walking. Keep cooling him on the drive, and let the vet check him even if he seems to improve.

Q: How can I help my hard of hearing dog hear better? I have a white bull-dog (we once thought it was a boxer) that is pretty deaf. He can hear some high pitched things it seems, but when asleep he …
A: While you probably can't actually help him hear better you can use alternative ways to communicate. I would recommend getting a collar that vibrates and to teach your dog that the vibration is the signal to come find you. That way you can get his attention even if he can't see you. Also work on hand signals so that once you have his visual attention you can communicate the rest of the command. Dogs tend to learn visual and motion queues faster than verbal only queues so once he is looking at you the rest should not be more difficult than normal training.

I would also highly reward him for voluntarily "checking in". Because you have to rely on visual queues you want your dog to prefer to keep you in his line of sight or frequently come to you to. So anytime he voluntarily does this without you giving a queue you should reward it.

A: No. There is no disease that has "no cure" (unless you were born with something like Down syndrome and such.)

People often say "it has no cure." What this really means is that they just can't cure it themselves. There is no saying your dog won't get over it by himself. Just because humans don't have a cure for it, doesn't mean it's incurable.

This is kind of a bad example: take for instance Ebola. It has "no cure" yet some people got over it themselves. Just because you got it doesn't mean you couldn't cure it. Let's hope for the best. Good luck.

A: The male sees the female cat as an invader or worse a prey. The same thing is valid for the female but the other way around. She believes she is in another cats territory so she will not attempt to fight back choosing to flee instead. As a result locking them in different rooms or allowing them to fight it out will not work as their mindset will not change.

You need to prepare a high space for the female cat so that she feels like she has a safe spot which will prevent her from fleeing and once the female cat starts viewing your house as her home rather than feeling like an invader your male cat will follow suit and won't attack her anymore.

Q: Where can I report animal abuse or neglect?
A: Under the Animal Welfare Act as amended by RA 10631 (Section 10):

- The Philippine National Police (PNP), the NBI and other law enforcement agencies have animal welfare enforcement officers
- The Secretary of Agriculture can deputize trained volunteers and members of NGOs and community groups as enforcement officers
- These officers can rescue maltreated animals and arrest violators

LGUs are also required to enforce the anti-cruelty rules of RA 8485 (RA 9482, Section 7). You can report to the police, your LGU, or an animal welfare group. Take photos or videos and note the date and place to help your report.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: How do I get my dog to stop stealing socks? My dog greatly enjoys stealing socks and running around with them in his mouth any chance he gets. He doesn't destroy them; he just holds on to them. Eventually, he …
A: Your dog is most likely stealing your socks because they smell like you. A few good ways to prevent this behavior are:
- Plenty of exercise. If your dog doesn't have loads of pent up energy, then he/she will be less likely to engage in extra-curricular activities.
- Attention. Have one-on-one time with your dog. After all he/she is stealing your socks for your smell, or, when you catch the dog in act, he/she will receive attention. Whether your reaction is good or bad, the dog still sees it as attention.
- Keep your socks out of reach. After all, if they aren't there, then they can't be stolen.

If you notice that the thieving sessions are around the same time every day, then you can easily prevent this by having a short 10-minute training or play session right around that time to distract your dog.

Hope this helps.

Q: Can cats see equally well in both light and dark? I know that the cats can see in the dark, but I have been wondering: can cats see as well in the dark as they do in the light? Or …
A: Cats can't literally "see in the dark", although they can see better in dim light than people can, because their pupils can expand to let more light in. So like us, they need some light, the more the better up to a point. (Glaring lights can make it as difficult to see as no light at all.)

A cat's vision is different than ours in other ways. Their colour vision is limited, and they are nearsighted. However, they are very quick to spot movement!

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

A: My guess is that your dog is drinking water as a nervous response to not being able to comprehend why the humans are moving around like that (they don't normally move like that)! Dogs with anxiety lick obsessively, tear things up, or develop other nervous 'ticks' (such as drinking water while under anxiety).

Look for other signs that your dog could be uncomfortable, and verify that this behavior is only triggered by certain circumstances (like the dancing).

If it's possible your dog is repeating this behavior more frequently (but maybe it was only first noticed during the dancing), consider a vet checkup, as it's possible there could be a more serious problem.

Q: How often does my dog need the anti-rabies shot by law?
A: Every year. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must have their dogs "regularly" vaccinated against rabies. The implementing rules make it clearer: a properly immunized dog is one vaccinated yearly, and LGUs register and vaccinate dogs annually.

The shot must be given by a licensed veterinarian, or by a trained vaccinator under a vet's direct supervision during government mass vaccination drives.

Keep the record of each shot on your dog's vaccination or registration card.

Q: What types of couch are resistant to damage from a cat? My orange tabby cat, Cheeto, is almost six years old. Right now in my living room I have three Ikea armchairs which are a simple wooden frame and cushions …
A: Most of all, your cat needs a suitable scratching post.

Cats will instinctively scratch on certain surfaces to sharpen their claws. In the wild, they prefer the bark of certain trees, but in human homes, they prefer fabric covered furniture. Even with severe and constant punishments, you will not keep a cat from scratching.

So as long as your cat doesn't have an alternative scratching surface, it will scratch your furniture. In my personal experience, it's best to offer some vertical scratching posts (usually integrated into a cat tree) plus one horizontal scratching mat (usually inexpensive cardboard mats).

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: Why do dogs yawn? My dog, who is a Black Mouth Cur, yawns sometimes. I can't figure out the reason. Note that yawning doesn't appear to be due to tiredness or the dog feeling sleepy, because it will yawn even …
A: Expanding on kmm's comment, kmm's link references Brainerd at al. (2004) whom conclude:

Yawing is common to all vertebrates and thus only seems to serve the purpose of stretching.

In general, yawing is a sign of high nitric oxide levels. Nitric oxide is also the hormone that results in blood-flow toward the genitals, and thus could just also be indicating that your pet is horny.

However, excessive yawning has been correlated with heart problems, and of course poor sleep (secondary ref here). If your dog does yawn excessively, and it doesn't seem to be correlated with poor sleep / loud snoring, it may be worth it to have them examined by a vet.

Enclosed litter boxes may be perfect for people, but not so much for cats. They are setups for ambushes. Kitties, instinctually, do not want to be in places where they can potentially be trapped. Even if there are no other threats or resident animals, instinct wins.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: When moving two cats in with different feeding styles, which should trump the other? My cat is currently fed on a twice daily schedule. I'm planning on moving him in with another cat who is currently free-fed. My cat will …
A: The problem with free feeding is that it requires you to use dry food (wet food will spoil if left out too long). Dry food does not contain the moisture that cats need and are accustomed to in their diets. Wet food is best, and so meal feeding is required.

Other reasons that meal feeding is preferred:
- Portion/Diet control. Many cats will eat all day and not exercise enough, becoming obese. This can also become important if one cat needs a special medical diet (allergies/intolerance is a common reason), or if the cats are at different weights and need different amounts of food.
- Monitoring ability. In a free fed multicat household, if one cat stops eating (or starts eating less) due to an illness/injury, it is much harder to detect.

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: Cat urinates where litter box was while litter box is being cleaned CAT: Male, 3-5 y/o, only cat, indoor only, above average weight, no known issues, 1 litter box. The last three times that I have done a deep clean …
A: A cat that feels secure in its environment may instinctively use the scent ot its waste to help mark its territory, in contrast to the instinct of an insecure cat to hide its scent. By washing the litter box so thoroughly, you are removing that scent and, by extension, his territorial claim. He needs to refresh his claim and, since the box is missing at the moment, he puts it on the floor in the same spot.

The simple solution is to lock him out of that room (or in another room) while you're cleaning the box. Expect him to use it again as soon as he's discovered what you've done.

Q: Which vaccines are core for dogs?
A: Core vaccines are the ones every dog should get, wherever it lives. For dogs these protect against:
- Distemper
- Parvovirus
- Adenovirus (infectious hepatitis)

Rabies vaccine is also core anywhere the disease is present or the law requires it.

Global guidelines now say leptospirosis vaccine should be given to all dogs in places where the disease occurs, so in those areas it is treated as core too.

Other vaccines, like kennel cough (Bordetella and parainfluenza), are "non-core". Your vet suggests them based on your dog's lifestyle, such as boarding or contact with many dogs. Ask your vet which vaccines suit your dog.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: Why does my cat fart a lot?

My cat farts a lot. In addition, his belly seems tight, like he's full of gas.

Should I be concerned about this flatulence?
A: Persistent flatulence is not normal. While an occasional fart is nothing to be concerned about, if it's happening daily then your cat should see a veterinarian.

Flatulence can have several different causes and only your vet can determine the cause for your cat.
- Overgrowth of the certain kinds of gut bacteria
- Intolerance to certain types of foods
- Irritable Bowel Disease (the intestines don't properly absorb food)
- Or other similar Gastrointestinal system problems.

Your vet may prescribe some over the counter medications to try, may do some bloodwork, and may recommend a biopsy to determine the cause of the flatulence.

Untreated GI problems can lead to malnutrition and discomfort for your pet, so it is important to get your cat to a veterinarian for proper care.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Q: My cat loves coconut oil. Is it safe to give him some? I use coconut oil to moisturize my skin everyday. If my cat happens to be around me by the time I'm using the coconut oil, he goes nuts …
A: I do not think giving your cat some coconut oil is dangerous in any way, and it does have some medical uses in pets.

But it is a type of fat, and you need to keep this in mind so your cat does not gain weight, so please limit the amount you give your cat.

One of the positive effects of giving coconut oil is a softer stool, and it can help your cat to pass hairballs a little easier.

You can use coconut oil on the cat's paws if they are sore, and it can be used to treat the cat's dry skin.

More information about this could be found in external articles: one at bostonstreetvet.com about usage of coconut oil for pet health and another one at organicfacts.com about usage of it in cats.

Remember that only clean, unaltered, food-grade coconut oil is safe for pets.

Q: Can cats occasionally be fed rice? My children fed our cat a snack 1 of cooked white rice and tuna. Is it healthy for my cat to eat rice? 1 In Australia, by snack, I do not mean a treat, …
A: My vet advises feeding rice and chicken for stomach/intestine upsets, so rice and tuna should be fine.

Just keep in mind that such food is NOT a balanced diet for cats and isn't good for long term use. An occassional treat or meal is fine. Most importantly, homemade diets generally lack enough taurine.

If taurine levels are deficient, the retinal cells of the eyes will eventually degenerate, impairing the vision. This condition is referred to as feline central retinal degeneration (CRD). Deficiency of taurine will also lead to a weakening of the muscle cells in the heart, causing a condition called dilated cardiomyopathy. Taurine is a component of bile salts, and its deficiency may cause digestive disturbances.

Source: Taurine in Cats

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

A: In games, your cat is learning skills that he will use throughout his life. When he accidentally corners himself, it's scary, and he reacts out of fear (by hissing).

As his guardian/playmate, if you respect his hiss and back off until he can uncorner himself and show interest in playing again, then he will learn that his verbal warning is effective. In the future, he will continue to use this warning (and not launch straight into a fight).

At the same time, he should also learn how not to corner himself (from these experiences), so you will see this happen less frequently as he grows up.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: What age do cats stop growing on average?

I've heard humans stop growing around age 18-24. What about cats? When do they stop growing in height?
A: There are a couple of growth periods for cats. The first takes about 4 months and takes them into the kitten stage. The second growth period of a kitten takes them from about 4 months to somewhere between 8 and 12 months to adult size depending on the size of the breed. Larger breeds will take longer to reach their adult size versus smaller breeds, but despite having adult size, they're still junior cats, they don't really become adult cats until their 3rd year.

I only mention the two growth stages (which are effectively continuous) because the dietary requirements change.

Q: Should I change my senior pet's food?
A: Maybe. Older dogs and cats have different needs:

Senior dogs:
- Usually need fewer calories, and gain weight easily
- May benefit from more fiber and good-quality protein to protect muscle

Senior cats:
- Often digest food less well, and may lose weight and muscle
- May need tasty, easy-to-digest, higher-protein food in smaller, more frequent meals

For both, aim for a healthy body shape, not too thin and not too heavy. Extra weight strains joints, while weight loss can be a sign of illness such as kidney disease.

Change foods slowly over several days. Ask your vet to check your pet's weight and muscle and suggest a diet that suits its health.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: How do I make veterinary syrup to mix with my cat's Metronidazole prescription? My cat was prescribed Metronidazole/Flagyl tablets and they taste horrific. I know there are compounding pharmacies that use veterinary syrup and would like to find a recipe. …
A: Short answer:

Crushing a pill and putting it in a home made syrup is a really bad idea.

Longer answer:

The digestive tract has different properties along its route. Different medications can have their usefulness significantly impacted by being available for absorption in different areas of the digestive tract.

To get the correct dosage to the patient many pills have a coating over them to ensure that the correct properties exist for them to be absorbed. When a compounding pharmacy creates a prescription syrup, they don't simply grind up the pill and put it in syrup, they create a complete solution that takes multiple variables into account.

Q: Why does my cat put toys in my shoes? My cat has a few favorite toys that he goes nuts for. More specifically: a plastic ball with a bell inside and a small stuffed mouse. From time to time when …
A: This is a common behaviour. There are a few different ideas as to why cats seem to like shoes in particular as stash locations.
- They are small spaces that seem hidden, which cats like - they want to hunt things and then hide them for later, and the shoes seem like a good sneaky way to hide them away from the other people in the house (or other animals), as they are small and hard to see into and easy to overlook.
- They are bringing you a present! Cats tend to hunt and bring the kills to whoever they care for (other cats, people, etc), and since your shoes will retain a lot of your personal scent, especially if they are ones you wear often, the cat will associate them with you, and thus put the toys there for you to find as gifts and proof of their hunting prowess.

Q: How can I find out if a dog I am considering is from a puppy mill? I am considering adopting a dog from a locally owned pet store, it a registered breed and has a pedigree. Is there any way …
A: The best way would be to visit the breeders, see the conditions that the dogs are kept in, and meet the parents. If the place seems clean and the adult dogs are sociable and have had some basic training, it's not a puppy mill.

If the breeder is too far away to visit, references from other breeders and puppy buyers are very useful. I'd also check out the breeder on Facebook, both the kennel page and their personal profile if you can find it. A pure money-making operation might have birth and death announcements, show results, and photos of dogs in a fenced yard or in kennels. What would be missing is evidence that the dogs are part of the family and regularly spend time interacting with people.

I'd also check out the breeder on Facebook, both the kennel page and their personal profile if you can find it. A pure money-making operation might have birth and death announcements, show results, and photos of dogs in a fenced yard or in kennels. What would be missing is evidence that the dogs are part of the family and regularly spend time interacting with people.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

A: Anything that you give to actively induce a bowel movement is likely going to be adverse for the cat.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: How can I tell if my dog or cat is overweight?
A: Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: My dog got into the trash and ate mouldy food. Now he's trembling.
A: Mouldy food, garbage and compost can contain mould toxins that cause tremors and seizures. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Signs often start within 1 to 2 hours but can take several hours. They include vomiting, shaking, wobbliness, a fast heartbeat, overreacting to touch or noise, and seizures.

Before and on the way:
- Don't make him vomit, especially now that he's trembling, because he could inhale it or have a seizure.
- Keep him in a quiet, safe spot away from stairs and edges.
- Tell the vet what he got into, such as old bread, dairy or compost.

With hospital care, tremors usually settle in 1 to 3 days. Use bins with secure lids and keep compost fenced off.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Can dogs eat yoghurt, is it good for them?

A: Actual natural yogurt's something that dogs in India have had as part of their diet for ages. Home made yogurt is... actually pretty easy but out of the scope for pets.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: My dog ate a few slices of raisin bread but he seems totally fine.
A: Please don't wait for signs. Raisins and grapes can cause kidney failure in dogs, so treat any amount seriously. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Vomiting or diarrhea often starts within 6 to 12 hours. Later signs include low energy, not eating, belly pain, weakness and drinking a lot. Kidney failure can develop within 1 to 3 days, and it is often fatal.

Before you go:
- Bring the bread or packaging so the vet can estimate how many raisins he ate.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm and note any vomiting or diarrhea to tell the vet.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

Q: Is it a good idea to get anti rabies vaccines or booster shots regularly for myself as well as my pets? I am new to taking care of or adopting puppies. I just adopted a 4 months old puppy, and …
A: All pets should be regularly vaccinated against rabies. Typically the first shot is done at a few months old, and additional shots are done every 1 or 3 years thereafter; your vet should track this and remind you when shots are due for each pet. Depending on where you live, doing this may be required by law, but even if not, it’s still a good idea. (There are also other vaccinations you should consider, but they vary by species.)

Human vaccination is much less common. The idea is that if you get bitten by an animal not known to be vaccinated, then you will tell a doctor immediately and get the necessary shots. However, if you live in an area where rabies is common or if you frequently handle strange animals, then ask your doctor about getting shots regularly just like your pets.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Can a cat get a sexually transmitted disease?

If my normally indoor cat mates with a feral cat, is it at risk of getting any diseases?

My cat has all of its vaccines up to date, so I suspect the only concern would be a sexually transmitted disease.

Inspired by a comment at the question Cat - How much time does anti-heat injections take to take effect?

The answer to this is yes this do happen but sex is only one way cats can get infected other types of close contact can spread diseases too.
- Feline herpes can be transmitted by body fluids.
- FIV cat aids can be transmitted by body fluids.
- Feline chlamydia can be transmitted by body fluids,
- Panelukopenia virus can be transmitted by body fluids.
- Calcivirus can be transmitted by body fluids.
- Catflu can be transmitted by body fluids
- Rabies can definitely be transmitted by body fluids and not only to other cats but to all types of animals including humans.

I assume there is several other types of illness that can be transmitted by body fluids not only from intercourse but from bites too.

Q: What is parvo and why is it an emergency?
A: Parvovirus is a very contagious virus that attacks a dog's gut. Puppies and unvaccinated dogs are most at risk. It spreads through infected poop and anything it touches, and it can survive in the environment for months or longer.

Signs usually start 5 to 7 days after exposure:
- Dullness, fever and not eating
- Then vomiting and diarrhea, often bloody

Dogs lose fluids fast and can go into shock. Some die within hours, but most dogs that get hospital care survive. See a vet now if your puppy has vomiting or bloody diarrhea. Call ahead so the clinic can protect other patients.

Keep sick dogs away from others. Ask your vet how to disinfect your home, because many cleaners don't kill parvo.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Q: Breeds of dogs for therapy

I am interested in and have been researching therapy dogs. I was wondering which breed of dogs make the best therapy dog and why?
A: It really depends on what kind of therapy. Best advice is to go to your area's website and explore what dogs they have, pictures, and if there are any adoptable career-change dogs. You can also talk to other people in that field about what breeds are best.

- German Shepard

Once you start talking about a more specific field, you'll start to see more breeds, but generally I feel these three are in just about every field.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

Q: My cat has round bald patches. Is it ringworm?
A: It might be. Despite its name, ringworm is not a worm. It is a fungal skin infection. Signs include:
- Round patches of hair loss
- Broken or stubbly hair
- Scaly, crusty or red skin
- Dandruff or extra grooming

Ringworm spreads to people and other pets, and children are at higher risk. Its spores can stay in a home for many months.

What to do:
- See your vet, since flea allergy and other problems can look similar
- Keep the cat in one easy-to-clean room during treatment
- Wash hands after handling her
- Clean and disinfect the home well

Treatment often takes six weeks or more.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: Do rabbits make any sounds?

I'm considering a pet rabbit and I am wondering about noise issues.

If dogs bark and cats meow, do rabbits make any noises, or are they silent?
A: For the most part rabbits are silent, but not entirely.

We've had three pet rabbits and they did, from time to time, grunt. Most of the time it was when they got irritated by the cats, but also when they decided that they didn't like something we were doing (like stealing their plastic keys). At any rate, the grunting sound is a sign of displeasure and a reasonable warning to stop what is bugging them and it's not terribly loud.

However, they'll not approach even the general noise level of regular cat and not even remotely close to a dog.

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: Does my indoor cat need vaccines?
A: Yes. The American Association of Feline Practitioners recommends core vaccines even for cats that never go outside. Core vaccines for cats cover:
- Panleukopenia (feline distemper)
- Herpesvirus
- Calicivirus
(these three come together as FVRCP)
- Rabies, where the disease is present or the law requires it

Feline leukemia (FeLV) vaccine is advised for kittens under 1 year. For adults it depends on risk, such as going outdoors or living with cats that do.

Good news for indoor cats: global guidelines say low-risk indoor adults usually need core boosters only every 3 years or longer.

Your vet will choose the vaccines and timing that fit your cat.

Q: Training a dog to "sit pretty" How would you proceed to obtain a nice "sit pretty" from your dog? Clicker training is about clicking the right "approximations" at the right moment. So what would be the sequence of approximations that …
A: Sit pretty is a very difficult thing for a dog to do and it's great exercise for them, especially if you ask them to alternate between "pretty" and "down."

In order to help the dog, I found it easier to start sitting with legs and feet in a "V" so the dog has something to lean against. Then you can ask for a hand touch (if they know it) and get them used to the idea of being in that position.

Eventually you can start reducing the amount of support and generalize in other areas like a corner and then a flat wall. Once they get the idea you can begin adding a "pretty" cue before they perform the maneuver.

Don't rush things and let your dog guide you as to when they are strong enough. Some dogs can pick it up quick and others need to build up their core a little more.

I and my wife are adopting our room mate's dogs, but they "insist" on sleeping in the bed with us because that is how they lived with my room mate. This would not be much of a problem if I could sleep okay with them. However, one of the dogs moves around a lot if I move, which wakes up frequently through the night. They also get fur in the bed. It causes me serious problems (e.g. dizziness, poor work performance, dangerous driving, etc...) if I am not able to sleep / sleep well.

Things we have considered:

If we leave them out in another room, they whine and try to break down the gates to come see us, which also keeps us up. My wife also won't stand for this solution because she does not want to see them upset (and I don't either, but I need to be able to keep my job, etc...).

I was thinking about getting dog beds beside our bed, but they probably will not stay in them. Temporarily, my wife is sleeping in the living room with them, or my room mate is sleeping with them, but neither of these are good long term solutions.

I have also considered giving away the dogs, but it has been my wife's "dream" to have dogs, and I do not want to crush her dream. This would be a last resort if all else fails.

Do you have any suggested solutions to this problem?

Look into crate training. It is a great solution and once crate trained the dogs really like their beds and sleep well. It also gives them a bed that they feel comfortable in away from home. It is important that you learn how to crate train an adult dog before you start though if these dogs have never been crate trained.

Feral Kitten With An Injury

So there's a family of kittens that has been living in my yard for a few months now. I've been feeding them daily and they recognize me, but they won't let me touch them or get too close.

Last week I noticed one of them was not using his front paw at all, lifting it up while he walked. I waited for a few days and it started to swell, so I tricked him into getting into a cage and took him to the vet to check him out. The vet noticed he had a puncture wound leaking pus, which she drained, and cleaned. The vet recommended I give him antibiotics lest the infection come back. I tried putting the antibiotic in his food, even mixing it with smelly things like sardines, but he can smell it and simply opts to eat his siblings food instead. I tried to capture him again to take him to the vet for boarding, so he can get an injectable antibiotic for a few days, but ever since that one time I caught him he's been very wary of me. He does not let me get any closer than 2 meters, and runs away to a neighbor's yard if I try to!

He still comes by to eat, and his paw, though he still doesn't bear weight on it, has not swollen anymore since the first vet visit, and he has started using it a little more for digging.

What are the odds this just clears up on it's own without antibiotics? I'm really struggling to capture him and I'm starting to think that if I keep trying to and failing it's just gonna drive him away!

To answer the question, you may have no choice but to trap him (a box trap is less stressful than chasing him) and keep him caged for the duration of treatment. Yes, he's likely to be unhappy about that and to sulk for a while after being released. Do you care more about his friendship or his health?

Q: How often should I bathe my Shih Tzu?
A: Most Shih Tzus do well with a bath every 3 to 4 weeks. Bathing too often can dry out their skin.
- Use a dog shampoo, not human shampoo
- Brush before the bath to remove tangles, then dry them fully, especially the ears
- Wipe the eyes and face daily, as tear stains and food build up there

Many owners keep a short "puppy cut" with a groom every 4 to 6 weeks, which makes daily care much easier.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: Do cat / pet sanatoriums exist? I just discovered that my kitten has FeLV. Because this is no longer a death sentence for her, I decided to keep her. She is an indoor cat with no external feline contact, and …
A: In german speaking countries (Germany, Switzerland, Austria and probably the Netherlands, too) there is the concept of "Gnadenbrot" (literally "bread of mercy"). It stems from medieval times when old people who were too old to work but had worked well in younger times still received payment in the form of bread.

This concept is now applied to farm animals who are too old or ill to work and would usually be slaughtered. These farms are called "Gnadenhof" (farm of mercy) and are usually quite small, ran by environmental or animal rights activists and absolutely dependant on donations. There are extremely few of those farms in Germany.

And there is the fact that animal protection laws in Germany forbid any shelter to kill animals for any other reason than a severe, incurable illness or abnormal behavior that causes suffering for the animal.

Q: At what age can my dog be considered old?

My dog is getting older but when would he be considered senior?

I know that 1 human year equates to 7 seven dog years.
A: When is a human considered to be old? The answer really depends on the individual.

The seven year rule is old and inaccurate. There are several other methods that take the life expectancy of dogs into account better, eg one dog-year equals five humans-years for small dogs and seven for bigger dogs. And then there are even some nonlinear metrics in determining a comparable age value.

If you and your dog think that he is old, ie he behaves like an old dog, treat him as such. I don't think it is good to treat a juvenile and active dog of high age as if he was a broken senile. Of course you still have to be careful as older dogs, no matter how active they are, will still have age-related problems and are more prone to injury than younger dogs.

Q: Can I give my cat human medicine?

Is it safe for me to use human medicine on my cat?

Are there occasions where it is OK to give my cat human medications?
A: Yes and No.

1) as user87 points out some human medications may be damaging to cats

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: Is there a genealogy test for pets? Is there a test out there like "23 and me" except for pets? Is there even anything out there like this? I would pay top-dollar to have this done. I'd like to see …
A: There are lots of them. Here are 3 in no particular order:
- catdnatest.org
- Veterinary Genetics Laboratory at the University of California
- Basepaws

You're looking at $100 and more.

These tests have been around a while. Here's an article from Wired magazine in 2012: New Genetic Test Reveals Your Cat's Ancestry and this blog post by Cherise Udell from 2013: Learn your Cat's Ancestry.

There are also many companies that check pet DNA for specific diseases, with PKD being the most important one for cats.

There are other pets and animals that can be tested as well, e.g. Embark or DNA My Dog for dogs, but also companies that do horses especially for horseracing pedigrees, cattle, swine, goats, llamas, etc. for animal breeding purposes.

I have never used any of them, so caveat emptor.

Q: Which vaccines are core for dogs?
A: Core vaccines are the ones every dog should get, wherever it lives. For dogs these protect against:
- Distemper
- Parvovirus
- Adenovirus (infectious hepatitis)

Rabies vaccine is also core anywhere the disease is present or the law requires it.

Global guidelines now say leptospirosis vaccine should be given to all dogs in places where the disease occurs, so in those areas it is treated as core too.

Other vaccines, like kennel cough (Bordetella and parainfluenza), are "non-core". Your vet suggests them based on your dog's lifestyle, such as boarding or contact with many dogs. Ask your vet which vaccines suit your dog.

Q: How can I encourage two cats to get along? In three days my friend is dropping off his cat so I can watch it for a week while he is on vacation. However, the last time I watched his cat …
A: Your cat is seeing your friend's cat as an intruder in his territory. It's natural for him to try to drive the intruder out.

I'd suggest the standard method: shut your friend's cat in a room with everything he needs and visit during the day. It's better if the room is one your cat doesn't spend much time in but not essential.

Generally after a few days your cat will have relaxed enough to accept the visitor, but if not, your friend's cat still has a safe place and is getting food, water and attention until your friend returns.

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

Q: I saw little white things like rice in my cat's poop. What is it?
A: Those are most likely tapeworm segments. They look like grains of rice or sesame seeds and may be stuck to the fur near the tail or in the poop. Cats usually get tapeworms by swallowing fleas while grooming or by eating mice or rats.

Other worm signs include:
- Vomiting or diarrhea
- A dull coat or potbelly, mostly in kittens
- Weight loss

See a vet today if you notice black, tarry poop, pale gums or weakness. Heavy hookworm or roundworm loads can cause serious blood loss, especially in kittens.

Bring a fresh stool sample to your vet. Treat for fleas too, or the tapeworms will come back.

Q: Which diseases can humans carry from cat to cat? I regularly pet and feed stray cats. Some of them live together and some live apart, so sometimes I touch two different cats that normally wouldn't interact with each other. Also, …
A: FIP is caused by infection with feline coronavirus (FeCV). From the National Library of Medicine:

"The most likely route of infection of feline corona virus (FeCV) is oral; therefore, cats from catteries and multi-cat household environments, where cats are shedding the virus in feces and sharing litter boxes, are at higher risk of being infected with the virus."

FeLV is another candidate, it is often called a "friendly disease" since sniffing each others noses or mutual grooming are sufficient to start the initial infection in the upper respiratory tract. The virus is also resilient enough to survive for at least 15 minutes on human skin or clothing and as such can be transferred from cat to cat by hitchhiking on the human, without the human being a host.

A: The primary reason for concern would be zinc toxicosis. This is basically the formation of zinc salts in the stomach acid which are toxic and can lead to diarrhea, lethargy, seizures, and more. It's quite dangerous and can require surgical intervention to treat.

Common sources of zinc poisoning in dogs and cats include the Lincoln penny(!) and zinc-oxide creams. Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: How do I transition my dog from using potty pads to going outside? I have a 2-year old Yorkie that I am having problems with potty training. I read in a few Yorkie books that we should start off by …
A: When you take him out, take a potty pad as well. Let him do his business on the outdoor potty pad. Start making the potty pad smaller, first cut it in half and just use half of it. Then keep using smaller and smaller pieces. Hopefully at some point he will transition from pad to grass as the target, but if not change from a potty pad to a tissue or some other biodegradable product.

If you place the potty pad in different areas you should have better results in the transition from pad to grass, though if you always place it in the same area it could make clean up easier. You will need to periodically adjust your training approach based on your dogs responses.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: Can I give moong dal (fried lentils) to dogs?

Can I give moong dal to stray dogs? Moong dal ingredients are Moong Lentis, Edible Vegetable Oil and Edible Common Salt.
A: Probably not.

Lentils on their own, properly cooked are probably fine. The fact that it's deep fried is probably not a good thing. And from my recollection, deep fried moong dahl's on the salty side, and too much salt is bad for dogs.

While Indian street dogs are hardy — it doesn't feel like the best idea, even if you have a big pile of 'em lying around. Junk food is as bad for them as it is for us.

Q: How can I tell if my dog or cat is overweight?
A: Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: Can my dog have a treat with medicine that she can only take on any empty stomach

Can I give my dog medicine with a little treat even if it says take on any empty stomach?
A: One treat still counts as "empty stomach", so yes. Especially if the dog refuses to take the medicine alone but does take it together with the treat, the benefits outweigh the negative effect one single treat can have.

However, you also need to wait a sufficient time after the last meal for the stomach to empty itself. Usually such medicine is best administered in the morning before the dog has breakfast.

Q: How often does my adult dog need booster shots?
A: It depends on the vaccine:
- Distemper, parvovirus and adenovirus: after the puppy series and an early booster (at about 6 months or 1 year old), modern vaccines protect for years. Global guidelines advise boosting no more often than every 3 years.
- Leptospirosis: protection is shorter, so it is usually given every year.
- Rabies: some vaccines last 1 year and some 3 years, but in the Philippines the rules of the Anti-Rabies Act (RA 9482) require a yearly anti-rabies shot.

Your vet will make a booster plan based on your dog's age, health, lifestyle and the products used.

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: What is a recommended amount of human contact necessary to socialize kittens? It is well-known that some human contact including petting and touching is necessary to socialize kittens to be comfortable around humans. I have no experience with this and …
A: E.B. Karsh did a study on the effects of human contact on kitten behaviour published in 1983. Some essential, and interesting, learnings from that include:
- Kittens handled only 15 minutes a day from birth through to 12 to 15 weeks would accept human affection, but would tend to wander and return rather than staying in place.
- Kittens handled for an hour or two for the same period would be sufficiently relaxed to curl up on people and sleep.

R.R. Collard, in 1967, noted that more handlers tended to make kittens more comfortable around humans.

There are a number of additional studies that show very early and regular handling have a positive effect on kitten development, so the upshot of it all is handle them frequently and for long durations right from the start all they way through their development.

I have no experience with this and work a day job, what is the typical amount of time I need to spend with them together or one-on-one from birth until 8 weeks+ to help prepare them for living with people?

E.B. Karsh did a study on the effects of human contact on kitten behaviour published in 1983. Some essential, and interesting, learnings from that include:
- Kittens handled only 15 minutes a day from birth through to 12 to 15 weeks would accept human affection, but would tend to wander and return rather than staying in place.
- Kittens handled for an hour or two for the same period would be sufficiently relaxed to curl up on people and sleep.

R.R. Collard, in 1967, noted that more handlers tended to make kittens more comfortable around humans.

There are a number of additional studies that show very early and regular handling have a positive effect on kitten development, so the upshot of it all is handle them frequently and for long durations right from the start all they way through their development.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.
