Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: Why do animals try to stay awake when they need sleep? I found a video on YouTube of animals drifting off and trying to stay awake (by jerking their heads etc. like humans do). Why do they do this instead …
A: Cat (and other animal) behavior is affected by many, sometimes conflicting, motivations. You can see the same behavior in people when they want to stay awake for some reason but are very short of sleep; when they start to fall asleep their head drops and they then snap their head up and attempt to stay awake again.

Cats prefer to sleep in locations they consider secure; if for some reason they are in a location where they feel threatened or can see possible prey, they wish to stay awake but if they need sleep they display this behavior. I have noticed this sort of falling asleep/trying to stay awake behavior is more common in kittens than in adult cats.

Q: My dog got into a plate of dark chocolate brownies. How worried should I be?
A: Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in. Dark chocolate, baking chocolate and cocoa powder are the most dangerous types because they contain the most theobromine, a stimulant dogs clear very slowly. Rich brownies are also fatty, which can trigger pancreatitis.

Signs can start within a few hours: vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, panting, drinking and peeing more, a racing heart, tremors and seizures.

Before you go:
- Note your dog's weight, the type of chocolate and how much he ate, and bring the wrapper or recipe.
- If the brownies were sugar-free, tell the vet, since xylitol is also dangerous.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Don't wait for signs to appear.

On the way, keep him calm and watch for shaking.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: How can I tell if my dog or cat is overweight?
A: Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

I am considering buying or adopting a new dog, and was wondering what signs I should look for to indicate health issues?
A: "Health issues" is such a broad brush... So, a general answer would be to examine the dog and make sure everything seems correct and use some common sense.

Are they clean, well kept, groomed, skinny/fat, breathing normally?

You can also get them out on a leash and make sure they walk/run correctly (no limping or favoring). Maybe let them out in a fenced area... watch for any signs of abnormal behavior.

Check the eyes, are they clouded or abnormal?

Generally spend some time with the dog and use your common sense.

If you are looking for a more specific health issue, list that in the question.

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

Q: Do old cats chase moving objects?

I know kittens usually like to chase moving objects, how about the old one? Do they also enjoy that?
A: Yes, older cats still love to play! The moving object simulates prey. A cat's natural instinct to hunt, chase, and pounce should never go away. They will slow down a little as they get older, but they should never lose the thrill of "the hunt."

Sometimes, it's up to us to make sure they don't slow down too much. We do this by providing different types of stimulation - all types of toys, things to scratch, and places to climb. Dragging string-type toys or feather wands are a great way to keep your older kitty's body and mind healthy.

Q: What is heartworm and how does my dog get it?
A: Heartworms are long worms that live in the heart and lung blood vessels. Dogs get them from mosquito bites, which pass on tiny larvae that grow into adult worms over about 6 months. Indoor pets are at risk too, because mosquitoes come inside.

Many dogs show no signs at first. Later signs include:
- A mild cough that won't go away
- Tiring easily or not wanting to exercise
- Weight loss and poor appetite
- A swollen belly

Sudden trouble breathing, collapse or dark brown urine is an emergency. See a vet now.

Experts advise prevention every month of the year and a heartworm test every year. Ask your vet for a preventive that suits your dog's weight and age.

Q: How can I tell if my dog or cat is overweight?
A: Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: Dog DNA test from stool not swabs

Does anyone know of a dog dna test that can provide heritage details from stool samples instead of by mouth swab?
A: It sort of depends on what your intent is. You can expect dog feces to be highly contaminated with DNA not from the dog, and therefore I would guess that you probably couldn't get a truly accurate DNA profile of the dog that way. However, if you already have accurate DNA profiles of dogs from mouth swabs, you may be able to get enough DNA from the feces to guess which dog in your database produced the waste with a reasonable level of accuracy. There are businesses that provide that service, with the intent of helping communal living spaces such as apartment complexes catch residents who aren't cleaning up after their pets. Poo Prints is one such business.

Q: How should I decide between a collar and a harness for a dog? Of all of the dogs that have been part of my family, we have only used collars for leashing. We've never had any negative experiences with them, …
A: A harness just puts the pressure of the leash around the strongest part of your dog's body. So, while the harness would technically be more comfortable for the dog, it will be less comfortable for you. A harness will help your dog control you better, rather than the control you're looking for.

The long-term solution is to train your dog not to pull on the leash. The ASPCA has lots of good guidance on that. Leash pulling is not necessarily a permanent behavior, regardless of whether you're using a collar or harness. It's possible to train it away, and that's the best solution.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: What are the signs of tick fever in dogs?
A: "Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

Q: my dog is having a seizure right now what do i do
A: Stay calm and focus on keeping him safe.

While it's happening:
- Move furniture and hard objects away. Only move him if he's near stairs, water or another danger.
- Keep your hands away from his mouth. He can't control his jaws and may bite without meaning to.
- Don't try to hold him down.
- Time the seizure, and take a short video for the vet if you can.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the seizure lasts more than about 3 minutes, if he has more than one in a row, or if he might have eaten something poisonous. Otherwise, call your vet soon after.

Afterward he may pace or seem confused. On the way to the vet, keep him calm, quiet and away from edges.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Go now if he is in severe pain. Go today if the ear flap suddenly swells up. Left untreated, ear infections can damage the eardrum and cause lasting hearing loss.

Q: Would my dog want to harm my guinea pig? I let my guinea pigs run around my room a little bit, and normally my dog will walk in the midst of them playing. I would expect it to be a …
A: The risk for guinea pigs is always high when mixing with dogs, simply because of their difference in size and guinea pigs' prey instincts that signal to any other animal that they are defenseless.

The exact degree of danger depends on the breed of your dog and how well trained your dog is. According to the American Kennel Club, Italian greyhounds:

are flash-and-dash coursing hounds with an instinct for pursuit.

This is a strong warning signal that your dog, while only part greyhound, will have a natural instinct to chase and even kill your guinea pig rather than befriend it. There are no guarantees, but if you love your pigs, it is best to keep them separate or keep your dog leashed at all times (and under supervision) when in a room together.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: Is a McDonald's hamburger safe for my dog?

I want to make my dog's birthday special.

Is it okay to give her just one McDonald's hamburger (and no more after that)?
A: Better safe than sorry and don't give it, lots of grease in these burgers! All that grease can cause a number of problems such as diarrhea or acute pancreatitis - which has a possibility of turning into a long term issue (most commonly seen in our small dogs). These burgers also contain onions which are toxic to dogs.

The other poster mentioned going to the pet store for a nice treat which is a good idea however stay away from bones:
- They damage teeth
- Break and puncture the intestinal track
- Break and cause an obstruction
- Get lodged in the roof of their mouth

A vet I work with had a case not too long ago with a bull pizzle that punctured the dogs esophagus and went into his chest cavity, the dog unfortunately passed away. Even though it's not technically a bone it's one of those scenarios to be weary of.

Q: How can I tell if my dog or cat is overweight?
A: Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

messages.content:
What is the appeal of the bath tub to a cat?

My 5 month old DSH spends several minutes, two or three times per day, playing in my bath tub. He'll be running around playing, then heads to the bathroom, jumps in, rolls around on the floor, paws at the drain and the fixtures, then moves on to something else.

He has never had a bath, though I have cleaned him using moist wipes made for cats. He has also never attempted this while the shower was in use. So I can't think of any reason he would have any emotions tied to the tub, positive or negative.

He does not seem to be hurting himself or anything, just getting a little moist from the residual water from the prior shower, and he doesn't seem to care. I'm fairly sure there is minimal chance he could ingest any soap residue from the tub floor, and even if he did it would be trace amounts and very dilute. (No more than I have accidentally rinsed into my mouth on rare occasions, and I survived.) So I haven't bothered trying to prevent this.

I guess I should note that he has many toys, and multiple sources of fresh drinking water, and uses them all.

Mostly I just want to know- why does he do it?

It may be because the tub smells like the household's humans, and the rolling is another way to pick up your scent.

Or it may be anything from temperature to "Boxes are fun!"

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: Are there rules on how my pet should be transported, like by van or boat?
A: Yes. Section 4 of the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485) sets rules for transporting animals:

- Carriers must provide clean, sanitary facilities for animals
- Animals must get food and water on trips longer than 12 hours, or when needed
- Overcrowding, cruel confinement and putting animals in vehicle trunks count as cruelty

A BAI permit is required to transport animals. For pets, apply for a BAI local shipping permit before your trip, and prepare a vet health certificate and rabies vaccination certificate.

Q: How can I medicate my big, strong cat when I can't get down on the floor? Stardust hiding in the closet. 18 pounds, 14 years old, very strong. I am 71 and have bad knees. I know what to do …
A: Day 1: Give her a small treat on surface that's at a convenient height for you to pill her (e.g., a shelf on a cat tree) -- but don't pill her yet. Do this a few times until she is relaxed about the whole thing. Then give the treat, pill her, and give her another treat.

Subsequent days: Give the treat, pill her, and give her another treat.

This should help in a couple of ways. The routine of treat-pill-treat lets her know what's about to happen. Even if the animal doesn't particularly like what you're about to do, that's less frightening than the unknown. The initial treat will make her come to you, and anticipation of the final treat will help calm her while you administer the pill.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

A: My parents dogs (which are litter trained) did that, too. So we changed the kind of the litter. We found a brand they did not eat, so everything is fine know.

Eating litter is something you should worry about, especially when it is clumping litter, because it can block his system. This depends on how much he is eating. So you should observe him until you found a brand you are sure he is not eating, and stop him whenever you see him chewing on the litter. A small amount should not be harmful, so don't panic, but watch him carefully.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

A: Others have already explained the theory behind why it generally works so I just wanted to add some additional info about what your expectations should be.

The Thundershirt requires at least a week or two of gradual training (if not more) to really get your cat comfortable with the idea of it. It's possible your cat will absolutely hate it at first so you should be ready with lots of patience when trying to train your cat to appreciate it. Also, some cats will just completely refuse wearing any kind of vest or harness so that is something you should be prepared for as well.

What could be easier is to train the cat not to fear car rides. This takes time as well, but could be more effective in helping your cat's anxiety. This will be easier if he's a kitten, but older cats can still be trained as well.

Q: Is dry food better for pets’ teeth? I had always heard that dry food was better for my dog and cat because it helps keep their teeth clean, I even remember TV commercials about dry treats that would clean the …
A: Trying to find some peer-reviewed article or book about the subject, I found "The Manual of Veterinary Dietetics," from Saunders / Elsevier.

The conclusion is that Soft vs Hard foods don't have any clear winner. Many studies were made or reviewed, and the authors found it hard to compare the conclusions because each study involved different animals, with different methods of analysis.

Those authors' conclusion was that animals of the same breed may have more tendency on developing dental problems since their anatomy is different, for example, having more or less space among the teeth.

Some special food (textured dry food), on the other hand, could be beneficial in the plaque removing process, and flat rawhide chews of small sizes could help too.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Go now if he is in severe pain. Go today if the ear flap suddenly swells up. Left untreated, ear infections can damage the eardrum and cause lasting hearing loss.

Q: My dog got hit by a motorcycle but he's walking and seems okay. Does he still need a vet?
A: Yes. Please take him to a vet now, even if he looks fine. Some injuries don't show their full effects for a day or two, and pale gums, fast breathing or weakness can be signs of shock or internal bleeding.

To get him there safely:
- Be careful, because a hurt dog may bite. Use a cloth muzzle only if he is breathing normally and has no chest injury.
- If he can't walk well, slide him onto a firm, flat surface like a board or folded blanket, and keep his head, neck and back as still as possible.
- Keep him calm and quiet, and have someone else drive.

Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic as you leave so they're ready for him.

Q: My cat is eating grass when take out for a walk

Whenever I take my cat out for a morning walk every now and then she starts eating grass. What may be the reason behind it? Is this normal?
A: Yes, this is normal, cats eat grass to get rid of hairballs, as grass makes them vomit and get rid of indigestible things they have eaten like the fur of prey they have eaten and their fur after they have washed themselves.

They can also eat grass to try to get rid of parasites like intestinal worms.

Some say cats eat grass to get some nutrients from it, but this is not likely as grass contains very little of nutritional value for a cat.

My cat starts looking for fresh grass as soon as the snow is gone in the spring. It is important to be sure the grass is as clean as possible, like after the rain and in a sandy type of soil.

Q: How can I tell if my pet's problem is a real emergency or can wait?
A: An emergency is any sudden, serious problem. If you're unsure, call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now. They can tell you whether to come in.

Go immediately if your pet:
- Has trouble breathing, breathes with the mouth open (cats), or has blue or very pale gums
- Is bleeding heavily
- Collapses, is unresponsive, or has a seizure
- Ate something poisonous
- Was hit by a vehicle or fell, even if they seem fine
- Is straining to pee with nothing coming out (especially male cats)
- Has a swollen belly and keeps retching (dogs)
- Suddenly acts very differently from normal

Save your vet's number and the nearest 24-hour clinic in your phone today, and know the route.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

A: There are several possible warming solutions, including putting a coat or sweater on your cat (purchased or homemade), an electric warming bed or heating pad (use the type intended for humans with caution-- they may get too hot and burn your cat), or an enclosed hideaway like a box, enclosed bed or cat house with warm blankets within. It should have a smallish opening and be not much bigger than the kitty to maximize conservation of body heat.

You can also possibly improve the indoor comfort by reducing drafts-- make sure that windows and doors are well sealed, or use any kind of calking, draft stoppers, or heavy window drape that makes sense for your home.

Also be sure to place as many as possible of your cat's important resources (like litter box, resting places, water bowl, scratching surface) in the warmest and least drafty parts of the house.
